###### Abstract

Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve
without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement
mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving
its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey
investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer
across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI
and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the
self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of
self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of
experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as
our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on
rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed
loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario
imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast
each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by
presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or
checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or
redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent
combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer
directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could
overturn these still untested verdicts.

## I Introduction

Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have fueled an explosive
proliferation of multimodal agents \[[1](#bib.bib2), [2](#bib.bib3),
[3](#bib.bib7), [4](#bib.bib238)\], spawning a flourishing spectrum of
self-evolution techniques across multimodal reasoning \[[5](#bib.bib45),
[6](#bib.bib48), [7](#bib.bib46), [8](#bib.bib47)\], multimodal
generation \[[9](#bib.bib63), [10](#bib.bib38), [11](#bib.bib163),
[12](#bib.bib99), [13](#bib.bib417)\], GUI and Web
navigation \[[14](#bib.bib42), [15](#bib.bib299), [16](#bib.bib135),
[17](#bib.bib293)\], and embodied manipulation \[[18](#bib.bib50),
[19](#bib.bib149), [20](#bib.bib231), [21](#bib.bib155)\]. Despite
strong scenario-specific gains, existing self-evolving methods are
designed and evaluated within single scenarios, and their mechanisms do
not transfer equally well in both directions of a scenario pair. For
example, majority voting derives label-free rewards for reasoning tasks
from consistency across sampled answers \[[22](#bib.bib43),
[5](#bib.bib45), [23](#bib.bib127)\], yet finds no counterpart in
embodied manipulation, where action trajectories admit no equivalence
check and physical rollouts incur steep execution and reset costs.
Conversely, world models circumvent expensive environmental interactions
via imagined rollouts \[[24](#bib.bib154), [25](#bib.bib311)\], but
raise a factor that is not scarce in reasoning, where sampling directly
from the policy costs little. Beneath this directional breakdown in
mechanism transferability, which suggests a cross-scenario asymmetry,
also lies a shared self-evolving loop across diverse tasks.
Specifically, across all four scenarios, self-evolving agents share the
same cycle, _i.e._, generating exploratory experience, acquiring
evaluative feedback, and consolidating persistent updates. This survey
investigates the structural source of cross-scenario asymmetry by
characterizing this shared loop and explaining why the two directions of
a scenario pair meet different obstacles to transfer.

However, as summarized in [Table I](#S1.T1 "In I Introduction"),
existing work leaves this cross-scenario asymmetry unaddressed. Primary
studies benchmark exclusively within specific
scenarios \[[40](#bib.bib166), [20](#bib.bib231)\], while prior surveys
either overlook the self-evolving loop as an analytical
object \[[1](#bib.bib2), [2](#bib.bib3), [3](#bib.bib7),
[41](#bib.bib68), [42](#bib.bib69)\] or formalize it as
scenario-agnostic \[[28](#bib.bib4), [31](#bib.bib5),
[33](#bib.bib237)\]. Even the closest related work \[[29](#bib.bib200)\]
attributes verifiable feedback and retraining costs to domain-level
paradigms, not to specific mechanisms. To fill this gap, we first
formalize the surveyed object through a genus and a differentia. The
genus comprises autonomous learning loops satisfying four criteria:
(_i_) _autonomy_, where the agent operates without human intervention
across goals, actions, feedback, and updates post-initialization; (_ii_)
_freshness_, where experience is generated under the current policy;
(_iii_) _durability_, where updates persist beyond the episode boundary;
and (_iv_) _recurrence_, where the loop iterates across cycles. The
differentia, _self-reference_, requires the agent to realize at least
one component of its own loop: the goal sampler, the feedback function,
or the evolution operator. Loops in the genus lacking self-reference,
termed fixed loops, serve as controls across all scenarios to
disentangle scenario-imposed constraints from the intrinsic effects of
self-evolution.

To locate where a mechanism can transfer, we adopt the three-stage
self-evolving loop as our analytical framework, decomposing each cycle
into experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update
consolidation. We formalize each stage’s bottleneck through two
governing factors: (_i_) rollout count and information gain, (_ii_)
feedback fidelity and credit localization, and (_iii_) retention and
generalization. Each scenario imposes ceilings on the rollouts
affordable per cycle ($`\bar{K}`$) and the feedback fidelity attainable
by admissible evaluators ($`\bar{F}`$), which span a two-dimensional
positioning matrix. In this matrix, multimodal reasoning is situated
where both ceilings are high, multimodal generation where $`\bar{F}`$ is
low, GUI and Web navigation where $`\bar{K}`$ is low, and embodied
manipulation where both are low, with simulation raising both ceilings.
Comparing self-evolving and fixed loops within each cell further
separates the limits imposed by scenario ceilings from those incurred by
self-evolving design, _e.g._, replacing answer keys with sampled
consensus in reasoning \[[22](#bib.bib43), [5](#bib.bib45)\]. The matrix
thus identifies which ceilings bind in each scenario, but alone cannot
determine whether a given mechanism is portable.

Building on this matrix, we formulate each self-evolving mechanism as a
trade-off, in which the agent raises a scarce factor by replacing a
fixed component with its own records, proposals, judgments, or memory
writes, at the price of presupposing a task-structural resource, such as
output equivalence or checkable outcomes. In a target scenario, a
mechanism is thus portable if the target holds this resource,
conditional if it holds the resource only for a sub-family or after
adaptation, blocked if the outcome to be judged is unobservable, and
redundant if the raised factor is not scarce. We attribute the
cross-scenario asymmetry structurally to the different combinations of
scarce factors and resources that the two directions of a scenario pair
encounter: _e.g._, voting finds no output equivalence in manipulation,
whereas world models raise a factor that is not scarce in reasoning.
These verdicts, inferred from single-scenario evidence and not yet
tested, define testable preconditions, not empirical guarantees. A gain
over a budget-matched ablation without self-evolution would overturn any
verdict that predicts no benefit from an unadapted transfer, which turns
these predictions into a concrete measurement agenda.

This paper makes four contributions, the first two to the survey and the
last two to the analysis.

1.  ✜
    A condition-based definition and paradigm demarcation. We
    operationalize autonomy and the differentia through a provenance
    matrix that records which party realizes each loop component, and
    apply the definition to sixteen neighboring paradigms, of which five
    fall outside the genus, two never satisfy the differentia, five are
    divided by it, and four are self-evolving by definition.
2.  ✜
    A stage-resolved review and positioning matrix. We review each
    scenario through the three-stage self-evolving loop, place the four
    scenarios in the positioning matrix, contrast self-evolving with
    fixed loops in each cell, and trace five degradation modes along the
    cross-cycle paths through which they propagate.
3.  ✜
    Directed portability across scenario pairs. We recast the mechanisms
    of all four scenarios as trade-offs and assign each a portability
    verdict for every target scenario, yielding a structural account of
    the cross-scenario asymmetry.
4.  ✜
    A falsifiable measurement agenda. We review the evaluation of
    task-solving capability, self-evolving capability, and judges, and
    identify the measurements whose absence leaves untestable three
    claims, _i.e._, that a gain stems from self-evolution, that a
    scenario occupies its assigned position, and that the verdicts hold.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
[Sec. II](#S2 "II Preliminaries") defines the surveyed object, and
[Sec. III](#S3 "III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop") develops the
three-stage loop and the positioning matrix.
[Secs. IV](#S4 "IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning"),
[V](#S5 "V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation"),
[VI](#S6 "VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation")
and [VII](#S7 "VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation") review the
four scenarios, and [Sec. VIII](#S8 "VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")
derives the portability verdicts. Finally,
[Sec. IX](#S9 "IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation") treats
evaluation, and [Secs. X](#S10 "X Open Challenges")
and [XI](#S11 "XI Conclusion") discuss open challenges and conclude.

## II Preliminaries

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Conceptually, a _multimodal agent_ is a goal-directed decision-making
system that interacts with an external environment through a closed
perception-cognition-action loop over heterogeneous observation and
scenario-specific action spaces \[[43](#bib.bib1)\]. We restrict the
scope to agents whose cognitive core is a large (multimodal) foundation
model \[[44](#bib.bib126), [45](#bib.bib124), [46](#bib.bib125),
[47](#bib.bib72), [48](#bib.bib73), [49](#bib.bib74), [50](#bib.bib75),
[51](#bib.bib107)\] extended via interface \[[52](#bib.bib15),
[53](#bib.bib16), [54](#bib.bib17)\], memory \[[55](#bib.bib57)\], and
tools \[[56](#bib.bib70), [57](#bib.bib71), [58](#bib.bib33),
[59](#bib.bib34)\], excluding architectures lacking such a core, such as
world-model planners and task-specific visuomotor policies. Since the
environment supplies perceptions, accepts actions, and specifies goals,
we adopt _multimodal agent-environment interaction_ as our formal
scaffold. To systematically diagnose the cross-scenario asymmetry, we
unfold this loop across two temporal scales: a _micro-scale_ capturing
step-by-step behaviors within a single episode, and a _macro-scale_
tracking the cycle-by-cycle evolution of the agent’s own components over
long-term experiences. The resulting dual-scale dynamics are formalized
under goal-conditioned partially observable Markov decision processes
(POMDPs) \[[60](#bib.bib12), [61](#bib.bib11)\]. On this scaffold, we
define the surveyed object across four levels, from the static agent and
environment through the learning loop and the autonomous learning loop
to the self-evolving loop.

### II-A Multimodal Agent

We formulate the static architecture of a multimodal agent as a
four-component tuple $`\mathcal{A}`$ ([Sec. II](#S2 "II Preliminaries"))
and its environment as a goal-conditioned, modality-decomposed POMDP
$`\mathcal{P}_{g}`$ ([Sec. II](#S2 "II Preliminaries")). The
multimodality condition of [Sec. II](#S2 "II Preliminaries") requires
$`\Phi_{\theta}`$ to directly encode or decode a non-textual channel
without intermediate text conversion, such as screen pixels, camera
frames, generated images or videos, or low-level motor commands. Under
this criterion, an agent perceiving a web page solely through its HTML
or accessibility tree is text-only despite rendered visual content.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Micro-Scale Interaction Loop.   Within one episode, shown in the
micro-scale panel of
[Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"),
the agent acts under a configuration $`\mathcal{A}`$ with its persistent
components
$`(\Phi_{\theta},\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{I})`$
held fixed, leaving only the short-term buffer
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}}`$ to evolve from initial state $`m_{0}`$.
The episode starts from $`s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}(\cdot\mid g)`$, runs over
$`t\in\{0,\dots,T-1\}`$, and terminates upon a stop action or horizon
limit $`T_{\max}`$, yielding a random stopping time $`T\leq T_{\max}`$.
Each step passes through the environment kernels and agent components:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
s_{t}\xrightarrow{Z}o_{t}\xrightarrow{\phi(\cdot,m_{t},g)}x_{t}\xrightarrow{\Phi_{\theta}^{\star}}y_{t}\xrightarrow{\rho}u_{t}\xrightarrow{P}s_{t+1},
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\phi`$ and $`\rho`$ are deterministic, $`Z`$,
$`\Phi_{\theta}^{\star}`$, and $`P`$ are stochastic, and the buffer
updates as $`m_{t+1}=\Psi(m_{t},o_{t},u_{t})`$. The fixed argument
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}}`$ in $`\phi`$ is suppressed per episode.
This synchronous discrete-time chain abstracts away the gap between
decision and control frequencies, which is immaterial for text actions
but adds per-rollout cost under real-time embodied control. Over the
micro-history $`h_{t}=(o_{0:t},u_{0:t-1})`$, the agent induces the
policy $`\pi_{\mathcal{A}}=\rho_{\sharp}\Phi_{\theta}^{\star}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(u_{t}|h_{t},g)\!=\!\Phi_{\theta}^{\star}\!\bigl(\rho^{-1}(u_{t})\,\big|\,\phi(o_{t},m_{t},g)\bigr),
``` |  | (2) |

where conditioning on $`h_{t}`$ suffices, fixed $`(\mathcal{A},m_{0})`$
and update $`\Psi`$ uniquely determining $`m_{t}`$ from $`h_{t}`$.
Compounded with environment transitions, this policy induces a
trajectory distribution $`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}}}_{g}(\tau)`$ over
$`\tau=(s_{0:T},\,o_{0:T-1},\,u_{0:T-1})`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}}}_{g}(\tau)\!=\!\mu_{0}(s_{0}\mid g)\!\!\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\!\!Z(o_{t}|s_{t})\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(u_{t}|h_{t},g)P(s_{t+1}|s_{t},u_{t}).
``` |  | (3) |

Goal-Conditioned Expected Return.  The loop induces the goal-conditioned
expected return

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\mathcal{A};\,g)\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\tau\,\sim\,p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}}}_{g}}\!\left[\,\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^{t}\,R(s_{t},\,u_{t},\,g)\,\right],
``` |  | (4) |

a performance functional of $`\mathcal{A}`$, not a quantity optimized
within an episode. Self-evolution modifies $`\mathcal{A}`$ between
episodes, as the macro-scale loop below formalizes.

### II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent

Informally, a self-evolving multimodal agent improves its persistent
components across cycles without human input post-initialization, learns
from experience generated under its own policy, and internally realizes
at least one improvement driver: selecting its goals, deriving its
feedback, or authoring its updates. We formalize the agent and its
environment as the triples $`\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{A}}`$
([Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")) and
$`\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{E}}`$
([Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 1: Dual-scale learning loop and its defining conditions. Within an
episode (green), $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ acts in $`\mathcal{P}_{g}`$ with
its persistent components fixed. Across episodes (blue), each cycle
samples goals with $`\sigma_{\omega}`$, scores the resulting batch
$`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ with $`V_{\nu}`$, and updates the agent with
$`f_{\zeta}`$
([Eq. 5](#S2.E5 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")).
Blue tags mark where each genus criterion applies, and orange SR tags
mark the meta-operators, at least one of which a self-evolving agent
must realize.

Macro-Scale Learning Loop.   Across episodes, the macro-scale frame
([Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"))
wraps interactions into agent-updating cycles. Starting from
$`\mathcal{A}_{0}`$, each cycle $`k`$ passes through goal sampling,
rollout, evaluation, and update:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}_{k}\xrightarrow{\sigma_{\omega}}\boldsymbol{g}_{k}\xrightarrow{p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}}}\mathcal{D}_{k}\xrightarrow{V_{\nu}}V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})\xrightarrow{f_{\zeta}}\mathcal{A}_{k+1},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$ denotes the goal batch drawn from
$`\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k})`$ with support
$`\mathcal{G}_{k}\!\subseteq\!\mathcal{G}`$, rollout law
$`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}}`$ applies
$`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g}`$ across each
$`g\in\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$, and $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ aggregates the
resulting goal-trajectory pairs (with single goals corresponding to unit
batch size). The history then extends to
$`\mathcal{H}_{k+1}=(\mathcal{A}_{0:k+1},\mathcal{D}_{0:k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{0:k}))`$,
recording realized scores, stochastic evaluator outputs being
non-recoverable from trajectories alone and failure-conditioned samplers
conditioning directly on realized values. We designate this recursive
mapping a *learning loop*. The term denotes the cross-cycle structure
without presupposing monotonic gains in
$`J(\mathcal{A}_{k};\mu_{\mathcal{G}})`$, and excludes within-episode
adaptation (*e.g.*, in-context learning), which remains confined to
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}}`$. A *cycle* is one iteration of this
mapping. When training proceeds in explicit rounds (each regenerating
tasks, evaluator states, or rollouts via the antecedent agent before
optimization), a cycle corresponds to one round, whose internal
optimizer steps form *within-cycle optimization* under $`f_{\zeta}`$. In
round-free regimes, such as online reinforcement learning drawing fresh
rollouts at every optimizer step, each step executes the full mapping as
a *degenerate cycle*.

Meta-Operators and Substrate.  We designate $`\sigma_{\omega}`$,
$`V_{\nu}`$, and $`f_{\zeta}`$ the three meta-operators of the loop,
each acting on whole episodes at the macro scale. Across multimodal
scenarios, the goal sampler draws from a fixed task
pool \[[62](#bib.bib161)\], poses questions about unlabeled
images \[[5](#bib.bib45)\], reselects GUI tasks by historical
success \[[17](#bib.bib293)\], or synthesizes simulated
scenes \[[63](#bib.bib116)\]. The feedback function verifies discrete
answers \[[64](#bib.bib176)\], inspects generated images via the
internal understanding pathway \[[10](#bib.bib38)\], queries a
vision-language judge on the final screen \[[14](#bib.bib42)\], or
evaluates simulator success predicates \[[62](#bib.bib161)\]. The
evolution operator updates $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ via policy
gradient \[[65](#bib.bib29)\] or writes lessons, skills, and memory
entries \[[66](#bib.bib255), [67](#bib.bib32), [68](#bib.bib10)\].
Auxiliary agents enter either as self-play opponents sampled via the
task argument
([Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")) \[[7](#bib.bib46)\]
or as learned proposer-solver roles instantiated within
$`\Phi_{\theta}`$ \[[22](#bib.bib43)\]. The *substrate* denotes the
persistent components that $`f_{\zeta}`$ modifies across
cycles \[[28](#bib.bib4), [31](#bib.bib5)\]. Specifically, a
*parametric* loop updates $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ alone, a *non-parametric*
loop modifies only $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}}`$, $`\mathcal{T}`$, or
$`\mathcal{I}`$ under fixed $`\theta`$ (training-free), and a *mixed*
loop alters both \[[69](#bib.bib233), [70](#bib.bib223)\].

Expected Evaluation Return.  We evaluate a learning loop at each cycle
via its expected return under the evaluation distribution
$`\mu_{\mathcal{G}}`$, which lies outside the control of
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ to prevent samplers from inflating performance
through easier goals. With cycles counted in rounds by some methods and
in optimizer steps by others, $`n`$ cycles span horizons of different
lengths, and the return is therefore reported per cycle. With
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ itself random, depending on the goals, rollouts, and
feedback recorded in $`\mathcal{H}_{k}`$, the expectation at cycle $`k`$
also ranges over this history,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{k}\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{H}_{k},\,g\,\sim\,\mu_{\mathcal{G}}}\!\left[\,J(\mathcal{A}_{k};\,g)\,\right],\quad k\in\mathbb{N}.
``` |  | (6) |

This sequence evaluates against the idealized reward $`R`$
([Eq. 4](#S2.E4 "In II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")), whereas
the loop ascends the proxy $`V_{\nu}`$.

### II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops

To distinguish it from general learning loops, we formalize the
self-evolving loop through a genus of four operational criteria and a
differentia of self-reference.

The Genus: Autonomous Learning Loops. We adopt four criteria to bound
the genus of autonomous learning loops. Autonomy bars human input across
all three meta-operators and rollout actions, whereas freshness,
durability, and recurrence respectively exclude static datasets,
episodic buffer writes, and uniterated single-shot updates:

1.  $`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$
    Autonomy.  Autonomy requires the loop to operate without human
    intervention across its meta-operators and action stream
    post-initialization. Formally, at every cycle $`k\!\geq\!0`$, the
    goals $`\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$, the signal
    $`V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})`$, and the update of $`f_{\zeta}`$
    consume no annotation, verdict, or approval added by a human while
    the loop runs, and no human-issued action, such as a teleoperated
    correction, enters $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$. Artifacts fixed prior to
    cycle $`0`$ (task sets, verification checkers, answer keys, external
    evaluators and judges, or optimizers) constitute the bootstrap.
    Human resets modifying $`\mathcal{P}_{g}`$ and not the learning loop
    itself, autonomy does not imply reset-free
    execution \[[71](#bib.bib35)\], and reset overhead is documented
    separately.
2.  $`\mathcal{C}_{2}`$
    Freshness.  Freshness requires per-cycle experience to be drawn from
    the agent’s current policy, not from a fixed dataset or an external
    stream. Formally, the cycle-$`k`$ distribution depends on
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ through $`\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}`$, admitting
    on-policy sampling
    $`\mathcal{D}_{k}\!\sim\!p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{\boldsymbol{g}_{k}}`$
    and asynchronous variants whose behavior policy lags
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ by a bounded number of updates, but excluding
    any agent-independent $`p_{\mathrm{static}}`$ \[[31](#bib.bib5)\].
    Experience collected once by $`\mathcal{A}_{0}`$ and reused in later
    cycles fails the criterion. Generating on-policy rollouts, however,
    satisfies freshness without constituting self-reference.
3.  $`\mathcal{C}_{3}`$
    Durability.  Durability requires the update to alter the agent
    beyond the episode boundary. Formally,
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}\!=\!f_{\zeta}(\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k}))`$
    must modify persistent components ($`\Phi_{\theta_{k}}`$, long-term
    memory $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{long}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{k}`$,
    toolset $`\mathcal{T}_{k}`$, or interface $`\mathcal{I}_{k}`$),
    thereby altering induced policy $`\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k+1}}`$ on at
    least one goal. This excludes adaptation confined to the
    within-episode buffer $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}}`$ and updates
    restricted to auxiliary proposers or evaluators, which belong to
    $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ yet occupy parameters that $`\pi_{\mathcal{A}}`$
    does not read, while admitting memory writes, tool additions, and
    prompt mutations even without any gradient
    descent \[[31](#bib.bib5), [34](#bib.bib8)\].
4.  $`\mathcal{C}_{4}`$
    Recurrence.  Recurrence requires the loop to close across cycles
    instead of terminating after a single update. Formally, the map
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k}\!\mapsto\!\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$ of
    $`\mathcal{C}_{3}`$ is iterated over more than one cycle, whether
    rounds or degenerate cycles, and each output becomes the next
    cycle’s agent, not a branch discarded after evaluation. This
    excludes single-pass optimization pipelines
    ($`\mathcal{A}_{0}\!\mapsto\!\mathcal{A}_{1}`$), even if compliant
    with $`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$ through $`\mathcal{C}_{3}`$. The criterion
    presupposes $`\mathcal{C}_{3}`$ and, being satisfied by every
    multi-step online method, discriminates loops only in round-based
    regimes.

The Differentia: Self-Reference. The four criteria constrain how the
loop runs, not who realizes it, a loop being able to satisfy
$`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$–$`\mathcal{C}_{4}`$ while every meta-operator is
realized outside the agent. The differentia, *self-reference* (SR),
separates self-evolving loops by requiring the agent to internally
realize at least one evolutionary meta-operator, marked by SR tags in
[Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries").¹¹
1 Our criteria adapt those of \[[31](#bib.bib5), [28](#bib.bib4),
[34](#bib.bib8)\] and treat updated components as a descriptive
substrate, but enforce a narrower scope. While prior work categorizes
learning from environmental or rule-based rewards as reward-based
self-evolution \[[31](#bib.bib5)\] or subsumes reinforcement learning
with verifiable rewards on fixed datasets \[[28](#bib.bib4)\],
self-reference excludes these regimes whenever the agent realizes zero
meta-operators. It does not require co-evolving environment
dynamics \[[34](#bib.bib8)\], evolving inter-agent
topologies \[[28](#bib.bib4)\], or lifelong operation ($`k\to\infty`$).
Self-reference and the meta-operator clause of autonomy both ask who
realizes each meta-operator, and we therefore record their evaluation
for a method $`m`$ in the *provenance matrix*
$`\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(m)\in\{0,1\}^{3\times 4}`$. Its rows index
$`(\sigma_{\omega},V_{\nu},f_{\zeta})`$ and columns span four provenance
classes: runtime human input (h), bootstrap artifacts fixed prior to
initialization (b), environment/task generation (e), and the agent (a),
with $`\Gamma_{ij}(m)=1`$ when class $`j`$ participates in realizing
meta-operator $`i`$ (rows admit multiple ones). Both conditions evaluate
over single columns:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{1}:\ \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(m)\,\mathbf{e}_{\text{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{h}}}}}}=\mathbf{0},\qquad\mathrm{SR}:\ \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(m)\,\mathbf{e}_{\text{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{a}}}}}}\neq\mathbf{0},
``` |  | (7) |

where $`\mathbf{e}_{\text{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{h}}}}}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{e}_{\text{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{a}}}}}}`$ select the h and a
columns, rendering the split between b and e descriptive. For example,
SimpleVLA-RL \[[62](#bib.bib161)\] realizes all three meta-operators
externally, whereas VisPlay \[[5](#bib.bib45)\] samples goals via an
internal Questioner within $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ and derives feedback from
votes over its own answers, the two matrices differing in the
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ and $`V_{\nu}`$ rows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\text{SimpleVLA-RL}}=\overset{\text{\makebox[5.0pt]{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{h}}}}}\hskip 6.0pt\makebox[5.0pt]{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{b}}}}}\hskip 6.0pt\makebox[5.0pt]{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{e}}}}}\hskip 6.0pt\makebox[5.0pt]{{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{{a}}}}}}}{\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&0\\
0&1&0&0\\

The a entry is tested under row-specific criteria. The goal-sampler row
is marked when $`\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k})`$ conditions on the
agent or its history, as with learned proposers, success-dependent
curriculum rules, or self-play opponents drawn via the task argument
([Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"));
post-hoc filtering of tied goals leaves subsequent draws unconditioned
and is excluded. The feedback row is marked when $`V_{\nu}`$ depends on
the agent, through the active policy (self-judges, consensus voting over
rollouts, or reward models refitted on trajectories) or frozen snapshots
(including the initial agent $`\mathcal{A}_{0}`$); group-relative
normalization and per-goal monotone transforms add no dependence.
Snapshots count because shared model lineage preserves priors, and
model-based evaluators reportedly favor their own
generations \[[112](#bib.bib36)\], a bias plausibly transmitted to
descendant policies. The evolution-operator row is marked when the agent
model, its replica, or an internally trained component writes update
content beyond raw rollouts, such as a lesson, skill, memory entry, or
relabeled goal. This row tests writer provenance, not functional
dependence, every $`f_{\zeta}`$ depending trivially on the updated
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$. Promptbreeder \[[109](#bib.bib30)\], which rewrites
its own improvement mechanism, is a special case of an a entry in this
row. Beyond membership, an a entry tracking the current agent couples
successive cycles through shared model parameters or history-conditioned
goal rules, whereas a frozen snapshot couples none.

Fixed Loops and Scope.  An autonomous learning loop with self-reference
is *self-evolving*, whereas one lacking it is *fixed-loop*, completing
the membership test in
[Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"). Because
the subsequent three-stage decomposition, its six factors, the two
ceilings, and cross-cycle coupling are defined over autonomous learning
loops, fixed-loop methods serve there as evidence characterizing a
scenario’s operating point, whereas scenario chapters review
self-evolving loops, reporting their provenance rows and design
variables. A method can have a entries in several rows (*e.g.*,
proposer-solver methods realize both the goal sampler and the feedback
function \[[22](#bib.bib43), [5](#bib.bib45)\]).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 2: The three-stage self-evolving loop and its six factors. Each
stage centers on one meta-operator, and its effectiveness
$`\mathcal{Q}_{k}`$ is the product of two factors. The filled ceilings
$`\bar{K}`$ and $`\bar{F}`$ serve as the axes of the positioning matrix
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).
The goal edge, fed by the trajectories and scores of cycle $`k`$,
reaches $`\sigma_{\omega}`$ only when it is adaptive, and extensions of
the agent edge into $`\sigma_{\omega}`$, FA, or UC are not drawn.

### II-D Demarcation from Established Paradigms

The term *self-evolving* shares vocabulary with several established
paradigms, and recent surveys draw its boundary at different
points \[[28](#bib.bib4), [31](#bib.bib5), [34](#bib.bib8),
[113](#bib.bib9), [114](#bib.bib61)\].
[Table II](#S2.T2 "In II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries")
compares adjacent paradigms; contested boundaries hinge on the a entry.
In the goal-sampler row, discarding tied groups within a batch adds no a
entry \[[62](#bib.bib161)\], whereas allocating subsequent rollouts by
task success qualifies \[[115](#bib.bib147)\]. In the evolution-operator
row, the test is who writes the update: a separate fixed model (*e.g.*,
GPT-4o guiding GPT-3.5-Turbo in TextGrad) keeps the loop
fixed \[[104](#bib.bib142), [102](#bib.bib258)\], whereas the acting
model itself, as with ExpeL’s insights \[[66](#bib.bib255)\] or STaR’s
rationales for failed instances \[[92](#bib.bib37)\], establishes
self-evolution. Reflexion \[[116](#bib.bib19)\], where the acting model
preserves self-reflections across episodic trials, qualifies as
self-evolving, although its reflections, written for one task, improve
no other task. Anti-forgetting mechanisms of continual learning map onto
the evolution operator $`f_{\zeta}`$, whereas classical curriculum
samplers such as POET \[[117](#bib.bib25)\], PLR and other regret-based
environment designers \[[118](#bib.bib89), [119](#bib.bib108),
[120](#bib.bib110)\], goal-proposing teachers \[[121](#bib.bib90),
[122](#bib.bib109)\], and expert-iteration and AlphaZero
self-play \[[123](#bib.bib248), [124](#bib.bib88)\] remain outside our
foundation-model scope.

## III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop

We adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop as our analytical framework,
decomposing each cycle of an autonomous learning loop into experience
generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation. Fixed and
self-evolving loops across all four scenarios sharing this structure, we
differentiate them by where the bottleneck binds instead of by topology,
treating rollout cost and feedback fidelity as bounds on viable
mechanisms. We first formalize the three stages and their governing
factors, then position the four scenarios within a positioning matrix
spanned by these bounds, and trace how the stages couple across cycles.

### III-A Loop Decomposition

As shown in
[Figure 2](#S2.F2 "In II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries"),
we factor each cycle into three scenario-invariant stages, each
organized around one meta-operator ($`\sigma_{\omega}`$, $`V_{\nu}`$,
$`f_{\zeta}`$). This decomposition applies across the entire genus of
autonomous learning loops and treats auxiliary operations, such as
credit assignment or data filtering, as refinements within a stage, not
as additional stages.

1.  Stage 1
    Experience Generation (EG):  the goal sampler $`\sigma_{\omega}`$
    draws the goal batch $`\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$, and the current agent
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ rolls out in $`\mathcal{P}_{g}`$ for each goal
    $`g\in\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$, producing the trajectory batch
    $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$. Through the quantity and informativeness of
    $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$, the only trajectories FA and UC act on, EG
    bounds how fast and how broadly the loop can evolve (*speed and
    breadth*).
2.  Stage 2
    Feedback Acquisition (FA):  the feedback function $`V_{\nu}`$ maps
    $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$, together with the agent history
    $`\mathcal{A}_{0:k}`$ when $`V_{\nu}`$ reads the agent, to scores,
    preferences, or critiques sourced from the environment, the
    bootstrap, or the agent itself. FA is the loop’s only source of
    information about the idealized task reward $`R`$ (*the
    $`R`$-aligned direction*).
3.  Stage 3
    Update Consolidation (UC):  the evolution operator $`f_{\zeta}`$
    computes an update from
    $`(\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k},V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k}))`$
    and writes it into at least one persistent component of
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$, producing the next-cycle agent
    $`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$. UC determines whether an update persists
    across later cycles and generalizes beyond the goals that produced
    it (*retention and generalization*).

The six factors originate at the two scales of
[Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries").
The per-episode cost $`c(\tau)`$ governing $`\bar{K}`$ and action
localization $`L_{\nu}`$ arise within the micro-scale interaction loop,
whereas information gain, evaluator fidelity $`F_{\nu}`$, and
consolidation factors ($`S_{\zeta}`$, $`G_{\zeta}`$) emerge from the
macro-scale learning loop, the positioning matrix thereby pairing a
micro-scale axis with a macro-scale one.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  MR |  MG |  GW |  EM |
| ① Quantity factor $`K_{k}`$:  how many rollouts can a cycle afford? |  |  |  |  |
|  ✜Cost of one rollout $`c(\tau)`$ |  one decoding pass |  one sampling pass or tool chain |  per-step environment latency |  per-step latency plus episode reset |
|  ✜Action recoverability |  none needed (no side effects) |  none needed (no side effects) |  partial (DOM and account-level writes) |  largely irreversible (contact, wear) |
|  ✜Reported wall-clock cost |  not reported per rollout (one pass) |  not reported per rollout (one pass) |  2.5–4.0 s per step \[[125](#bib.bib144)\], episodes of tens of minutes \[[115](#bib.bib147)\], 5–10 min environment re-initialization per training step \[[15](#bib.bib299)\] |  about 20 h per real-world experiment with human resets \[[19](#bib.bib149)\], 2.6–16.9 s per judge query \[[21](#bib.bib155)\] |

|  ✜Interaction mode |  single action, sometimes tool-integrated |  single output or a short tool chain |  multi-step screen states, partially observable |  multi-step physical states, partially observable |
|  Primary bottleneck of $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}}`$ |  Quality, at saturation |  Quality |  Quantity |  Both, on hardware |

TABLE III: Asymmetric substitutability of
$`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}}`$ across four scenarios. Profiling
experience generation across the quantity and quality factors from
[Eq. 9](#S3.E9 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop").
The bottom row highlights the binding bottleneck for each scenario,
showing where cheap rollouts saturate and where costly environments

### III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG)

EG produces the trajectory batch $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ of each cycle by
rolling out the current agent $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ in the POMDPs
$`\mathcal{P}_{g}`$ of
[Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"). For
each goal $`g`$ in the batch $`\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$ drawn from
$`\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k})`$, $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ draws
$`K_{k}`$ rollouts from $`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g}`$ and pools them
into $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$. EG must supply experience of sufficient
*scale* and *informativeness* under finite compute, wall-clock, and
safety budgets, a constraint on quantity and one on quality. We
summarize this bottleneck through an effective-experience decomposition,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}}\;:=\;K_{k}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\sigma_{\omega}(k,\mathcal{H}_{k})}\!\left[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(g)\right],
``` |  | (9) |

where $`K_{k}`$ is the number of per-goal rollouts in cycle $`k`$, and
$`I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(g)\!:=\!\mathrm{Var}_{\tau\sim p^{\pi}_{g}}[\mathrm{ret}_{g}(\tau)]`$
is the outcome variance of $`g`$. Here,
$`\mathrm{ret}_{g}(\tau)\!=\!\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},u_{t},g)`$
denotes the return of $`\tau`$, and $`p^{\pi}_{g}`$ abbreviates
$`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g}`$. This variance, a goal-level proxy for
the learnable information gain \[[131](#bib.bib56)\], vanishes on goals
that $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ has mastered or never solves, where GRPO-style
group-relative updates receive zero advantage under an $`R`$-aligned
evaluator. Under a binary terminal reward with $`\gamma\!=\!1`$, it
reduces to $`p_{g}(1-p_{g})`$, which difficulty-targeting rewards and
filters track via an estimated success probability $`p_{g}`$. Defined on
the idealized reward $`R`$ of
[Eq. 4](#S2.E4 "In II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"), the proxy
renders $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{EG}}`$ diagnostic, and it exposes two
failure modes. As $`K_{k}`$ shrinks, too few per-goal rollouts remain to
contrast success with failure. As $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$
approaches zero, the sampled goals are mastered or unreachable.
Concretely, $`K_{k}`$ is bounded by per-rollout *interaction cost* and
*action recoverability*, while $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ is
governed by the *diversity and information gain* targeted by
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ and by the *interaction mode* realizing
$`p^{\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}}_{g}`$
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).

Quantity Constraint.   Interaction cost and action recoverability govern
$`K_{k}`$ via a single per-rollout cost $`c(\tau)`$, eliminating the
need for a separate term for actions that resist reverting, resetting,
or safe repetition. Specifically, $`c(\tau)`$ absorbs the time, compute,
synchronization, and reset cost of one rollout, with the reset term
penalizing both environment restoration and expected damage from failed
trajectories. Under a fixed per-goal budget $`B`$, the rollout count
satisfies the affordability ceiling
$`K_{k}\!\leq\!\bar{K}\!:=\!B/\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[c(\tau)]`$, where the
expectation runs over episodes of the target task family at the horizon
cap $`T_{\max}`$, not over the rollouts of a particular policy, which
lets $`\bar{K}`$ reflect task structure and not policy choice. When
$`c(\tau)`$ is small, group-sampling operators such as
self-consistency \[[80](#bib.bib96), [132](#bib.bib111)\] or
GRPO \[[65](#bib.bib29), [133](#bib.bib112), [134](#bib.bib113)\] sample
a group of rollouts per goal at negligible marginal cost. As $`c(\tau)`$
grows, the bottleneck shifts from theoretical execution feasibility to
the budget of exploratory failures the system can absorb.

Quality Constraint.   Even with a large $`K_{k}`$, a trajectory set is
unproductive if its goals are already mastered or still unreachable for
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$, leaving EG viable only while
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]\!>\!0`$. For instance,
self-play \[[131](#bib.bib56)\] stops improving once its synthetic
pipeline no longer supplies learnable information gain. *Diversity and
information gain* determines whether $`\sigma_{\omega}`$ draws goals
with nonzero $`I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}`$. Sampling schemes escalate in
intervention from random sampling \[[65](#bib.bib29)\] through
curriculum mining over past failures \[[135](#bib.bib139),
[17](#bib.bib293)\] and active task selection \[[136](#bib.bib114),
[137](#bib.bib118)\] to environment synthesis \[[63](#bib.bib116),
[138](#bib.bib117), [139](#bib.bib229), [140](#bib.bib302),
[141](#bib.bib102)\]. Random sampling keeps $`\sigma_{\omega}`$
stationary, whereas curriculum mining and active selection make it
adaptive. Environment synthesis acts through the task argument $`g`$ of
[Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries") and is
adaptive only when the generator reads the agent’s record. Only an
adaptive sampler conditions the next goal draw on the agent’s record and
places an a entry in the goal-sampler row. *Interaction mode* fixes what
evidence each trajectory can expose. Single-pass generation and
tool-augmented reasoning yield single-action episodes, whereas digital
and embodied environments expose multi-step state transitions whose
informativeness depends on platform dynamics, reset conditions, and
observability.

Asymmetric Substitutability.   The product in
[Eq. 9](#S3.E9 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
enables mutual compensation between its two factors, locating the
cross-scenario asymmetry in the cost of raising each factor. Raising
$`K_{k}`$ offsets low information gain only when rollouts are cheap,
parallelizable, and recoverable and feedback retains contrast as group
size grows. Consensus rewards losing contrast beyond small
groups \[[22](#bib.bib43)\], the loop elsewhere must instead raise
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ via curriculum
mining \[[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293)\], active
exploration \[[5](#bib.bib45), [18](#bib.bib50)\], demonstrations at
initialization \[[19](#bib.bib149)\], or synthetic
environments \[[6](#bib.bib48), [63](#bib.bib116), [138](#bib.bib117)\].
Equal values of $`K_{k}`$ therefore do not imply identical bottlenecks.
Multimodal generation and GUI/Web navigation report overlapping group
sizes
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
yet generation samples cheap, reversible passes below $`\bar{K}`$ and is
bounded by $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ over a fixed prompt pool,
whereas navigation incurs latency-bound episodes and is bounded by
$`\bar{K}`$ itself. Cheap but uninformative rollouts saturate the loop,
whereas informative but costly rollouts throttle its scaling.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  MR |  MG |  GW |  EM |
| ① Fidelity factor $`F_{\nu}`$:  how faithfully does $`V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})`$ order trajectories by $`\mathrm{ret}_{g}`$? |  |  |  |  |
|  ✜Signal source (provenance) |  majority vote a, self-judgment a, computed answers e |  self-rewards a, same-model judges a, external judges b |  task checkers b, VLM judges b, co-evolving RMs a, same-model judges a |  episode outcomes e, progress heads and same-model judges a, VLM judges b |
|  ✜Channel coverage |  full (discrete answer) |  often perceptual only |  full on screen, partial for backend state |  full in simulation, visual only on hardware |
|  ✜Gaming resistance under $`f_{\zeta}`$ |  high for computed answers, untested for votes |  low \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165)\] |  untested beyond downstream success \[[142](#bib.bib193)\] |  low without judge oversight \[[143](#bib.bib206)\] |
| ② Localization factor $`L_{\nu}`$:  how finely can credit be apportioned along $`\tau`$? |  |  |  |  |
|  ✜Temporal granularity |  episode $`=`$ step ($`T\!=\!1`$ without tool calls) |  episode ($`T\!=\!1`$ if single-pass) |  episode (judges), step (co-evolving RMs) |  episode (outcomes), step (progress heads) |
|  ✜Credit-assignment cost |  none ($`T\!=\!1`$) |  none if single-pass, low otherwise |  co-trained step RMs \[[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143)\] |  demonstration-trained progress heads \[[19](#bib.bib149), [145](#bib.bib52)\] |
|  Primary bottleneck of $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}}`$ |  Realized $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ |  Fidelity ceiling $`\bar{F}`$ |  Localization |  Both, on hardware |

TABLE IV: Asymmetric vulnerability of $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}}`$
across four scenarios. Profiling feedback acquisition across the
fidelity and localization factors from
[Eq. 10](#S3.E10 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop"),
with signal sources tagged by provenance. The bottom row identifies the
binding bottleneck for each scenario, showing where gameable signals
misdirect the loop and where coarse signals under-constrain it.

### III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA)

FA maps the trajectory batch $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ of each cycle to the
feedback
$`V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})\!\in\!(\mathbb{Y}^{\mathrm{mm}})^{*}`$, the
scores, preferences, critiques, or structured judgments that direct
$`f_{\zeta}`$. Any scoring, ranking, filtering, or best-of-$`N`$
selection by $`V_{\nu}`$ belongs to FA even when interleaved with
generation, whereas $`V_{\nu}`$-independent filtering such as
deduplication remains in EG. FA must supply feedback that is *aligned*
with the intended objective $`R`$ and *localized* at an actionable grain
without recurring human supervision ($`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$), a constraint
on fidelity and one on localization. We summarize this bottleneck
through an effective-feedback decomposition,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}}\;:=\;\bigl(2F_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k};R,\boldsymbol{g}_{k})-1\bigr)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{D}_{k}}}\!\left[L_{\nu}(\tau)\right],
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{D}_{k}}`$ is the empirical measure on
$`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$, $`F_{\nu}\!\in\![0,1]`$ is the rate at which the
ordering $`V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})`$ induces on same-goal trajectory
pairs agrees with their ordering by $`\mathrm{ret}_{g}`$, and
$`L_{\nu}(\tau)\!\in\!(0,1]`$ is the fraction of environment actions
along $`\tau`$ to which $`V_{\nu}`$ can assign credit. Here, pairs tied
under either ordering are excluded, and $`F_{\nu}\!:=\!1/2`$ if none
remains. This pairwise form covers scalar, pairwise, and ranked feedback
alike, and $`2F_{\nu}-1`$ is the Goodman-Kruskal rank correlation of the
two orderings, zero for a random evaluator and negative for a reversing
one. Like $`I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}`$, $`F_{\nu}`$ is defined on $`R`$,
which makes $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{FA}}`$ diagnostic, and it exposes
two failure modes. As $`F_{\nu}`$ falls toward $`1/2`$, $`f_{\zeta}`$
follows an uninformative proxy, and below $`1/2`$ it optimizes against
$`R`$. As $`L_{\nu}`$ shrinks, a correct signal becomes too coarse to
guide improvement. Concretely, $`F_{\nu}`$ is bounded by the *signal
source* and *gaming resistance* of $`V_{\nu}`$, while $`L_{\nu}`$ is
governed by the *temporal granularity* and *credit-assignment cost* of
its scores
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).

Fidelity Constraint.   Signal source and gaming resistance act on
$`F_{\nu}`$ at different levels: the signal source fixes the evaluator
configurations $`\Xi_{V}`$ a scenario admits, hence the
attainable-fidelity ceiling
$`\bar{F}\!:=\!\sup_{\nu\in\Xi_{V}}F_{\nu}`$, whereas gaming resistance
governs how much of it survives repeated $`f_{\zeta}`$ updates. Where a
closed-form success condition or a discrete answer space exists,
deterministic instruments such as answers computed by task
generation \[[64](#bib.bib176), [146](#bib.bib175)\], unit
tests \[[147](#bib.bib119), [148](#bib.bib120)\], and
physical-constraint rewards \[[18](#bib.bib50), [145](#bib.bib52),
[149](#bib.bib53)\] sustain high $`F_{\nu}`$ at modest cost. Lacking
both, evaluators rely on self-rewards \[[9](#bib.bib63),
[10](#bib.bib38), [150](#bib.bib378), [151](#bib.bib379)\], reward
models \[[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143), [152](#bib.bib49),
[153](#bib.bib93), [154](#bib.bib115), [155](#bib.bib380),
[156](#bib.bib381)\], or VLM judges \[[14](#bib.bib42),
[18](#bib.bib50), [157](#bib.bib234), [158](#bib.bib382)\], and gaming
resistance binds \[[9](#bib.bib63), [159](#bib.bib67)\]. *Channel
coverage* further caps $`F_{\nu}`$, an instrument leaving unobserved
channels of $`\mathcal{U}`$ unconstrained \[[9](#bib.bib63),
[18](#bib.bib50), [145](#bib.bib52)\]. Self-rewards and co-trained
reward models read $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ and place an a entry in the
feedback row, and their realized fidelity $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ therefore
drifts with the policy they score; all others enter as b or e. Reported
audits measure label or verdict accuracy $`a`$, not the pairwise
agreement that defines $`F_{\nu}`$. Under a binary terminal reward with
verdict errors independent across trajectories and symmetric across
outcomes, a success-failure pair is ordered correctly with probability
$`a^{2}`$ and reversed with probability $`(1-a)^{2}`$, giving
$`F_{\nu}=a^{2}/(a^{2}+(1-a)^{2})`$, which exceeds $`a`$ whenever
$`a>1/2`$. A reported accuracy thus bounds $`F_{\nu}`$ from below only
under these assumptions, and errors correlated within a goal void the
bound. In multimodal reasoning, program-computed answers stay correct on
94.4% of retained questions \[[64](#bib.bib176)\], yet self-generated
pseudo-labels degrade across rounds \[[5](#bib.bib45),
[160](#bib.bib204)\], consistent with self-referential evaluators
drifting below a high $`\bar{F}`$, although rising question difficulty
confounds these declines.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  MR |  MG |  GW |  EM |
| ① Retention factor $`S_{\zeta}`$:  does the cycle-$`k`$ gain survive subsequent updates? |  |  |  |  |
|  ✜Dominant substrate |  $`\Phi_{\theta}`$, except training-free methods |  $`\Phi_{\theta}`$, or $`\mathcal{M}`$, $`\mathcal{T}`$, $`\mathcal{I}`$ if training-free |  $`\Phi_{\theta}`$, or $`\mathcal{M}`$, $`\mathcal{T}`$ if training-free |  $`\Phi_{\theta}`$, or $`\mathcal{M}`$, $`\mathcal{T}`$, $`\mathcal{I}`$ |
|  ✜Iteration robustness under $`f_{\zeta}`$ |  untested beyond a few cycles |  compounding hacking within single runs \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165)\] |  sustained by trajectory replay \[[14](#bib.bib42), [17](#bib.bib293)\], no forgetting on held-out environments \[[15](#bib.bib299)\] |  fixed-loop continual RL only \[[95](#bib.bib59), [161](#bib.bib60)\] |
|  ✜Dominant failure mode |  long-cycle drift |  compounding reward hacking |  distribution shift |  forgetting and distribution shift |
| ② Generalization factor $`G_{\zeta}`$:  does the gain transfer beyond $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$? |  |  |  |  |
|  ✜Transfer locus |  parameters (any goal) |  parameters, or memory and skills (on use) |  parameters, or memory and skills (on use) |  parameters, or skills and harnesses (on use) |
|  ✜Experience coverage in $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ |  tasks synthesized over unlabeled media |  a fixed prompt pool |  the evaluation task set or stream \[[162](#bib.bib137), [163](#bib.bib228), [104](#bib.bib142), [164](#bib.bib230)\] |  one simulator suite |
|  ✜Achieved generalization scope |  cross-task \[[7](#bib.bib46), [5](#bib.bib45), [22](#bib.bib43)\] |  in-distribution, partly cross-benchmark \[[129](#bib.bib165), [165](#bib.bib222)\] |  in-distribution, one platform |  in-distribution, rare sim-to-real \[[166](#bib.bib156), [18](#bib.bib50)\] |
|  Primary bottleneck of $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}}`$ |  Retention |  Retention |  Generalization |  Generalization |

TABLE V: Within-regime specialization of
$`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}}`$ across four scenarios. Profiling
update consolidation across the retention and generalization factors
from
[Eq. 11](#S3.E11 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop"),
both lacking a scenario-fixed ceiling. The bottom row identifies the
binding bottleneck for each scenario, showing where later cycles erode
gains and where updates stay within sampled goals.

Localization Constraint.   Even with high $`F_{\nu}`$, a trajectory set
is directionally unproductive if $`L_{\nu}`$ covers a vanishing fraction
of environment actions, and FA accordingly remains viable only while
$`\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[L_{\nu}(\tau)]`$ suffices for the grain
$`f_{\zeta}`$ requires. *Temporal granularity* fixes the scoring unit
along $`\tau`$: the terminal outcome for episode-level scores, the
action $`u_{t}`$ for step-level scores, and the output $`y_{t}`$ decoded
into $`u_{t}`$ for token-level scores. Because $`L_{\nu}`$ counts
environment actions, a single-action episode has $`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$, and
credit within a long reasoning chain $`y_{t}`$ lies outside $`L_{\nu}`$
even where process reward models assign it \[[153](#bib.bib93)\].
Episode-level feedback suffices when the task reduces to one discrete
outcome, step-level process supervision becomes necessary as horizons
lengthen and terminal success grows too sparse \[[153](#bib.bib93),
[167](#bib.bib92), [168](#bib.bib55), [18](#bib.bib50),
[169](#bib.bib383)\], and token-level credit remains rare outside
independently checkable reasoning chains \[[170](#bib.bib44)\].
*Credit-assignment cost* determines how much of that grain a cycle can
afford, step-level scores requiring a process model or per-step
estimates whose cost grows with horizon length \[[153](#bib.bib93)\].
Granularity is thus an FA choice that reaches $`f_{\zeta}`$ only through
its signal.

Asymmetric Vulnerability.   The product in
[Eq. 10](#S3.E10 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
admits only conditional, one-directional compensation between its two
factors. Higher $`F_{\nu}`$ from cross-model verification or
understanding-generation duality offsets moderate localization loss only
when an unbiased anchor exists \[[10](#bib.bib38), [128](#bib.bib39)\],
whereas finer $`L_{\nu}`$ yields no directional gain once $`F_{\nu}`$ is
gameable \[[9](#bib.bib63), [159](#bib.bib67)\]. Equal ceilings
$`\bar{F}`$ therefore do not imply identical bottlenecks. Multimodal
reasoning and GUI/Web navigation both admit a high $`\bar{F}`$
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
through program-computed answers \[[64](#bib.bib176)\] and per-task
state scripts in sandboxed environments \[[115](#bib.bib147),
[17](#bib.bib293)\], yet reasoning fixes $`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$ and is
bounded by the realized $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ of its consensus and
self-judged signals \[[5](#bib.bib45), [160](#bib.bib204),
[171](#bib.bib209)\], while navigation scores whole long-horizon
episodes and is bounded by $`L_{\nu}`$ \[[16](#bib.bib135),
[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143)\]. Multimodal generation instead
faces a low $`\bar{F}`$ on open-ended prompts, where self-rewards and
perception-only instruments are readily gamed \[[9](#bib.bib63),
[10](#bib.bib38)\], and embodied manipulation loses both factors on
hardware \[[172](#bib.bib153), [173](#bib.bib160), [19](#bib.bib149),
[145](#bib.bib52)\]. Fidelity-bounded signals thus misdirect the loop
and localization-bounded ones under-constrain it, making $`\bar{F}`$ a
positioning axis and $`L_{\nu}`$ a within-regime variable.

### III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC)

UC writes the update that $`f_{\zeta}`$ computes from
$`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ and $`V_{\nu}(\mathcal{D}_{k})`$ into one or more
persistent components of
$`\mathcal{A}_{k}\!=\!(\Phi_{\theta_{k}},\mathcal{M}_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k},\mathcal{I}_{k})`$,
as $`\mathcal{C}_{3}`$ requires. Writes to the episode-scoped buffer
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{short}}`$ through $`\Psi`$ fall outside UC, and
$`V_{\nu}`$-based selection of what to write remains in FA. UC must
write updates that *persist* undegraded across subsequent cycles and
*generalize* beyond the cycle-$`k`$ goals, a constraint on retention and
one on generalization. We summarize this bottleneck through an
effective-consolidation decomposition,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}}\;:=\;S_{\zeta}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{k:k+j+1}\bigr)\cdot G_{\zeta}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{k+1};\,\mu_{\mathcal{G}}\bigr),
``` |  | (11) |

where
$`\Delta_{k}(g)\!=\!J(\mathcal{A}_{k+1};g)\!-\!J(\mathcal{A}_{k};g)`$ is
the cycle-$`k`$ gain on goal $`g`$, $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$ is the support
of $`\boldsymbol{g}_{k}`$, and $`\mu_{\mathcal{G}}`$ is the fixed
evaluation distribution of
[Eq. 6](#S2.E6 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries").
Here, $`S_{\zeta}\!\in\![0,1]`$ is the fraction of the cycle-$`k`$ gain
on $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$ that survives $`j`$ further cycles,
$`\min\{1,\,\max\{0,\,\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mu_{\mathcal{G}}|\mathcal{G}_{k}}[J(\mathcal{A}_{k+1+j};g)-J(\mathcal{A}_{k};g)]\,/\,\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mu_{\mathcal{G}}|\mathcal{G}_{k}}[\Delta_{k}(g)]\}\}`$
for a positive denominator, and $`G_{\zeta}\!\in\![0,1]`$ is the
$`\mu_{\mathcal{G}}`$-measure of goals outside $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$ with
$`\Delta_{k}(g)\!>\!0`$, renormalized to the complement of
$`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$. The gain and the two factors correspond to the
adaptivity, retention, and generalization goals proposed for
self-evolving agents \[[31](#bib.bib5)\], and $`S_{\zeta}`$ normalizes
by the cycle-$`k`$ gain the change on earlier goals that backward
transfer records as a signed difference \[[94](#bib.bib27)\]. Like
$`F_{\nu}`$, both factors are defined through $`J`$ and hence on $`R`$,
leaving $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\mathrm{UC}}`$ diagnostic as well, and it
exposes two failure modes. As $`S_{\zeta}`$ falls toward zero, later
cycles erase or distort the cycle-$`k`$ gain. As $`G_{\zeta}`$ falls
toward zero, the update stays confined to $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$.
Concretely, $`S_{\zeta}`$ is bounded by the *substrate* that
$`f_{\zeta}`$ writes and its *iteration robustness*, while $`G_{\zeta}`$
is governed by the *transfer locus* of that substrate and the
*experience coverage* of $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).

Retention Constraint.   Substrate and iteration robustness act on
$`S_{\zeta}`$ at different levels: the substrate fixes how far a single
write can interfere with earlier gains, whereas iteration robustness
governs whether those gains survive repeated $`f_{\zeta}`$ applications.
The substrate is either $`\Phi_{\theta}`$, written by
GRPO \[[65](#bib.bib29)\], PPO \[[174](#bib.bib6)\], or
DPO \[[175](#bib.bib28)\], or a non-parametric component such as
memory \[[55](#bib.bib57), [176](#bib.bib18), [116](#bib.bib19),
[177](#bib.bib384), [178](#bib.bib385)\], tools \[[67](#bib.bib32),
[179](#bib.bib31)\], or prompts \[[180](#bib.bib58), [181](#bib.bib14),
[182](#bib.bib13)\]. Three documented failure modes threaten iteration
robustness: compounding reward hacking through accumulated Stage 2 bias
within single runs \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165)\], distribution
shift as the rollout law leaves the calibration region of
$`V_{\nu}`$ \[[14](#bib.bib42)\], and catastrophic forgetting through
interference in $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ \[[95](#bib.bib59),
[161](#bib.bib60)\]. Hacking and shift enter across the cycle boundary,
whereas forgetting arises inside $`f_{\zeta}`$ and yields to experience
replay, parameter isolation, and regularized updates \[[95](#bib.bib59),
[161](#bib.bib60), [183](#bib.bib77), [184](#bib.bib78),
[185](#bib.bib79), [186](#bib.bib76)\]. Within one task family, the
three modes can compound into *long-cycle drift*, a slow multi-source
degradation that terminal-only reporting leaves undetected and per-round
scores on a fixed benchmark suite reveal only as non-monotone curves.

Generalization Constraint.   Even with high $`S_{\zeta}`$, a persisted
update confers no broader benefit if it improves only the goals in
$`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$, UC thus remaining useful only while
$`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$ improves on a non-trivial share of the goals
outside $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$. *Transfer locus* fixes where a write takes
effect: on any goal that activates the affected weights for parameters,
upon retrieval for memory, upon invocation for tools, and within the
templating scope for prompts. *Experience coverage* determines the
subspace of $`\mathcal{G}`$ to which the update can generalize, and
reported gains stay mostly within the support of $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$, as
the fixed loops UI-Voyager \[[187](#bib.bib136)\],
UI-Mem \[[104](#bib.bib142)\], and an online skill
library \[[164](#bib.bib230)\] train and evaluate on the same task sets.
Achieved scope rises from in-distribution transfer to unsampled goals of
the same regime, through cross-task transfer to neighboring goal
subspaces, to cross-domain transfer to other GUI platforms or real
hardware, the last reached by few methods on small trial
counts \[[166](#bib.bib156), [18](#bib.bib50)\]. The substrate thus
upper-bounds transfer, and the coverage of $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ sets how
much of it a cycle realizes.

Within-Regime Specialization.   Neither factor of
[Eq. 11](#S3.E11 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
has a scenario-fixed ceiling, and UC therefore specializes within each
quadrant, not along an axis. $`S_{\zeta}`$ binds when FA is gameable or
EG is non-recoverable, and $`G_{\zeta}`$ binds when $`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$
covers too little of $`\mathcal{G}`$. Shared substrates therefore do not
imply identical bottlenecks. Multimodal reasoning and GUI/Web navigation
share $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ as the dominant substrate
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
yet reasoning sustains intensive parametric writes under low-cost EG and
rule-checkable FA and is bounded by long-cycle drift \[[5](#bib.bib45),
[22](#bib.bib43), [64](#bib.bib176)\], while navigation stabilizes its
parametric writes by trajectory replay \[[14](#bib.bib42),
[17](#bib.bib293)\] and, in both parametric and training-free forms, is
bounded by transfer that stays within one platform. Multimodal
generation shares the retention bottleneck through compounding hacking
of its parametric writes \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165)\], and
embodied manipulation shares the generalization bottleneck, writing to
$`\Phi_{\theta}`$ and to skills, memory, and
harnesses \[[188](#bib.bib150), [189](#bib.bib152), [190](#bib.bib151),
[166](#bib.bib156)\] within single simulator suites. Few methods measure
either factor across cycles, and retention on earlier-round goals is
measured in a single self-evolving loop, RSI in
UMMs \[[191](#bib.bib216)\], besides fixed-loop continual reinforcement
learning \[[95](#bib.bib59), [161](#bib.bib60)\]. UC thus inherits its
bottleneck from the first two stages and refines a method within its
quadrant without moving it.

Fig. 3: Cross-scenario positioning matrix. The axes are the
scenario-fixed ceilings $`\bar{K}`$ and $`\bar{F}`$, both decreasing

### III-E Cross-Scenario Positioning

The stage analyses locate where each scenario’s loop is bound, and this
subsection condenses them into a positioning matrix that accounts for
the cross-scenario asymmetry. To serve as an axis, a stage factor must
be *scenario-exogenous*, fixed by task structure instead of algorithmic
choice, and *substitution-resistant*, bounded in a way that the paired
factor of its stage cannot relax. Realized values, which each method
sets through its budget and evaluator, fail the first condition, leaving
the ceilings as the only admissible axes.

Axis Selection.   We select the ceilings $`\bar{K}`$ and $`\bar{F}`$ as
the two axes, the only stage factors satisfying both conditions. The
horizontal axis $`\bar{K}`$ is fixed by interaction cost and
recoverability, and no information-gain intervention lifts it. With
$`B`$ shared as a comparison convention, not a measured quantity,
$`\bar{K}`$ orders scenarios by $`\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[c(\tau)]`$. The
vertical axis $`\bar{F}`$ is fixed by verifier availability, and no
localization refinement raises it. We assess $`\bar{F}`$ on the task
families that define a scenario’s target, such as open-ended prompts in
generation and open task sets on hardware in manipulation, excluding
sub-families whose closed-form success predicates push the ceiling near
one. Its value is the highest fidelity a reported evaluator attains on
these families, an estimate that may run high, agreement measured on
fixed outputs tending to fall under optimization. The other four factors
each fail a condition: the information gain fails scenario-exogeneity,
its ceiling $`\sup_{\omega}\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ being set
by backbone coverage; the localization $`L_{\nu}`$ fails
substitution-resistance in that a higher $`F_{\nu}`$ offsets its deficit
when an unbiased anchor exists; and $`S_{\zeta}`$ and $`G_{\zeta}`$ have
no scenario-fixed ceiling.

|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Failure mode |  Cross-cycle mechanism |  Surfaces at |  Carried by |  Primary mitigation locus |
|  ①Compounding reward hacking |  An FA fidelity deficit inside $`V_{\nu}`$’s calibration support, tolerable per cycle, re-amplifies into a directional bias |  UC |  Agent edge, into FA if $`V_{\nu}`$ reads $`\mathcal{A}_{k}`$ |  Tighten $`F_{\nu}`$ at FA, or shrink the update step |
|  ②Distribution shift |  Rollouts drift off $`V_{\nu}`$’s calibration support, where its errors are extrapolations |  FA |  Agent edge, environment path |  Recalibrate $`V_{\nu}`$ at FA, or resample in EG |
|  ③Forgetting and plasticity loss |  A moving goal distribution makes writes to $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ interfere, erasing earlier skills and eroding plasticity \[[192](#bib.bib269)\] |  UC |  Environment path, goal edge |  Replay earlier goals in EG, or isolate or reset parameters |
|  ④Curriculum collapse |  $`\sigma_{\omega}`$ contracts the goal support toward mastered regions, causing $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ to decay |  EG |  Goal edge, or agent edge into $`\sigma_{\omega}`$ |  Inject exploration into $`\sigma_{\omega}`$, or score goals by difficulty |

TABLE VI: Cross-cycle degradation modes. Each failure mode is
characterized by its mechanism, the stage where it surfaces, the path
that carries it, and where it is primarily mitigated, all inferred from
within-run, fixed-loop, and out-of-loop evidence.

Quadrant Assignment.   We place each scenario in a quadrant of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
by the height of its two ceilings, calling a ceiling binding when it is
low. Multimodal reasoning faces neither low ceiling, multimodal
generation a low $`\bar{F}`$ on open-ended prompts, GUI/Web navigation a
low $`\bar{K}`$ under latency-bound episodes in sandboxed environments
whose end states per-task scripts inspect, and embodied manipulation
both in physical deployment, its target. Three displacements, drawn
dashed in the matrix, qualify this placement: (*i*) most embodied loops
learn in simulation, where success predicates raise $`\bar{F}`$ and
group sampling eases $`\bar{K}`$, shifting the operating point toward
the navigation cell; (*ii*) generation contains verifiable sub-families
such as OCR-scored prompts \[[195](#bib.bib173), [196](#bib.bib386),
[197](#bib.bib387), [198](#bib.bib388), [199](#bib.bib389)\] and
program-rendered charts \[[191](#bib.bib216)\], raising $`\bar{F}`$
toward the reasoning cell; and (*iii*) navigation on live websites or
free-form goals lacks state scripts and falls to screenshot
judges \[[101](#bib.bib134), [200](#bib.bib140), [201](#bib.bib298)\],
lowering $`\bar{F}`$ toward the manipulation cell. The four scenarios
thus occupy four quadrants, consistent with the bottom rows of
[Tables III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
and [IV](#S3.T4 "Table IV ‣ III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop"),
and the two off-diagonal cells, cheap but gameable generation and costly
but verifiable navigation, are combinations that a single difficulty
ordering would merge. In the absence of any study that estimates either
ceiling under one definition in more than one scenario, the placement
remains inferred from reported operating points.

Backbone Prior as a Confound.   The backbone $`\mathcal{A}_{0}`$
confounds this placement by bounding what a loop can reach independently
of task structure. In text-only models, self-verification sharpens a
model toward outputs it already ranks highly \[[202](#bib.bib249)\],
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards narrows the problems
solved at large sampling budgets \[[203](#bib.bib250)\], and gains from
spurious rewards vary with the model family \[[204](#bib.bib251)\].
Backbones also differ across scenarios, from vision-language models
pretrained on large question-answering corpora in reasoning to action
policies with far less motor pretraining in manipulation. Part of the
contrast that the matrix attributes to $`\bar{K}`$ and $`\bar{F}`$ may
thus reflect backbone coverage, a factor that stays entangled with task
structure.

Feasibility Filter.   The matrix supplies the first of two checks on
whether a mechanism transfers across scenarios. Scenario-fixed by
construction, the two ceilings bound the rollouts and the fidelity open
to any learning loop within a quadrant. A transferred mechanism further
presupposes resources of its source scenario that neither ceiling
records, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and where the
target lacks them, the mechanism is conditional on an adaptation or a
sub-family that supplies them. The matrix thus bounds within-cycle
feasibility without deciding portability, its verdicts remaining
untested while each reported comparison stays confined to one scenario.

### III-F Cross-Cycle Coupling

Beyond the matrix’s within-cycle bounds, the recurrence of
[Eq. 5](#S2.E5 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")
couples successive cycles. It feeds two cycle-$`k`$ outputs into Stage 1
of cycle $`k{+}1`$, the updated agent $`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$ that induces
the next rollout policy and the extended history $`\mathcal{H}_{k+1}`$
that conditions the next goal draw, each defining a directed edge across
the cycle boundary. Environmental drift, which
[Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries") holds
fixed but live websites exhibit \[[200](#bib.bib140),
[205](#bib.bib62)\], enters as a third path from outside the loop. These
paths carry both self-reference and long-run degradation.

Two Coupling Edges.   The two edges differ in carrier and
conditionality. The *agent edge* runs from Stage 3 of cycle $`k`$ to
Stage 1 of cycle $`k{+}1`$, carrying the persisted update into
$`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$ and hence into the rollout distribution of
$`\mathcal{D}_{k+1}`$. Present in every autonomous learning loop, it
supplies the closure on which $`\mathcal{C}_{4}`$ rests and extends to
any further component that reads the current agent: to
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ under a trained proposer \[[22](#bib.bib43),
[5](#bib.bib45)\], to Stage 2 under an evaluator sharing
$`\Phi_{\theta}`$ \[[22](#bib.bib43), [6](#bib.bib48)\], rendering
$`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ endogenous, and to Stage 3 under a generative model
that records lessons or skills \[[20](#bib.bib231),
[162](#bib.bib137)\]. The *goal edge* runs from Stages 1 and 2 of cycle
$`k`$ to Stage 1 of cycle $`k{+}1`$ through
$`\sigma_{\omega}(k{+}1,\mathcal{H}_{k+1})`$, carrying the cycle-$`k`$
trajectories and their scores into the next goal draw. A stationary or
scheduled sampler, reading no cycle-specific signal, leaves this edge
inert, whereas an adaptive sampler activates it and superimposes a
second feedback loop on the agent edge. Self-reference thus acts through
the extensions of the agent edge and through the goal edge: a fixed-loop
method retains only the agent edge into Stage 1, and a frozen snapshot
satisfies self-reference without opening any of these paths.

Five Degradation Modes.   We interpret long-run degradation through
these paths under a *mitigation-locality reading*, in which the stage
where a degradation surfaces, the path that carries it, and the stage
where it is best mitigated need not coincide, and
[Table VI](#S3.T6 "In III-E Cross-Scenario Positioning ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
records all three for five modes. Compounding reward hacking and
distribution shift travel along the agent edge as the in-support and
extrapolation variants of Goodhart’s law \[[206](#bib.bib254)\], which
reward-model overoptimization exhibits together \[[207](#bib.bib253)\],
with shift also entering along the environment path \[[14](#bib.bib42),
[200](#bib.bib140)\]. Forgetting and plasticity loss follow a moving
goal distribution carried by the environment path or the goal
edge \[[192](#bib.bib269)\], and the two collapse modes contract the
support of EG, curriculum collapse through the goal edge or the agent
edge into $`\sigma_{\omega}`$ \[[131](#bib.bib56), [5](#bib.bib45)\] and
model collapse through the agent edge under any
sampler \[[193](#bib.bib267)\]. The three loci diverge most for hacking
and forgetting, which both surface at UC yet admit remedies upstream of
the symptom, a tighter $`F_{\nu}`$ at FA \[[9](#bib.bib63)\] and replay
in EG. Long-cycle drift compounds the first three modes within one task
family and forms no sixth mode. The agent-edge extension into UC, absent
from the table, surfaces through erroneous writes, within a single pass
in Mobile-Agent-E \[[162](#bib.bib137)\] and across later rollouts in
SEAR \[[20](#bib.bib231)\]. With existing loops running only a few
rounds, these mechanisms are inferred from within-run and fixed-loop
evidence, and the reading stops at the cycle boundary.

Scenario Exposure.   The scenarios engage these paths unequally. In
reasoning, a learned proposer extends the agent edge into
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ and pass-rate curricula open the goal
edge \[[208](#bib.bib278), [209](#bib.bib281)\], both inviting
curriculum collapse. Reasoning and generation both extend the agent edge
into FA through self-referential verifiers, yet the outcome follows
$`\bar{F}`$: under reasoning’s high ceiling, $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ drifts
below $`\bar{F}`$, whereas under generation’s low ceiling, compounding
hacking sets in unless a frozen judge cuts that extension. In navigation
and manipulation, task or environment changes drive shift and forgetting
along the environment path and agent edge, and costly rollouts limit the
EG resampling that counters them. Coupling thus extends the asymmetry
across cycles.

## IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning

Multimodal reasoning occupies the quadrant of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
in which neither ceiling is low, its rollouts being single decoding
passes and its short answers admitting exact match against a
pre-collected or computed reference. Training against pre-collected keys
under a stationary sampler forms a fixed loop, from which self-evolving
methods depart along two branches. Weight-updating loops mostly pose
their own questions or train on unlabeled ones, letting the agent’s
outputs supply most answers and tying the evaluator to the model it
trains, which makes the realized fidelity $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$, not
$`\bar{F}`$, the binding factor. Training-free loops keep a frozen VLM
with the key or a program and let the agent write the skills or tools it
reuses, several gating each write against a validation reference, moving
the cost of self-reference to the frozen writer. Reported loops run
within one training run, over up to nine rounds of weight updates or
sixteen of training-free writes, or over one pass of a benchmark stream.
````
