### IV-A EG Bound by Informative Goals

Experience generation in multimodal reasoning draws goals that pair a
visual input (an image, a video clip, or frames of a 3D scene) with a
question whose short final answer admits an equivalence check. The task
families center on visual question answering over mathematical, chart,
and diagram inputs \[[240](#bib.bib121), [241](#bib.bib122),
[242](#bib.bib123)\], extending to pairwise quality
judgments \[[211](#bib.bib178)\], temporally grounded video
questions \[[160](#bib.bib204), [127](#bib.bib213)\], metric spatial
questions over 3D scenes \[[235](#bib.bib214)\], and physical dynamics
in videos \[[239](#bib.bib280), [226](#bib.bib279),
[209](#bib.bib281)\]. These goals come from a dataset, a fixed
generator, or generative roles of the agent, and in weight-updating
loops the solver typically answers each goal in $`K_{k}`$ independent
decoding passes, occasionally with tool calls, yielding a
$`\mathcal{D}_{k}`$ that groups answers to the same question, whereas
training-free loops run the frozen VLM on each goal with its current
skills, tools, or notes.
[Table VII](#S4.T7 "In IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning")
summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of
[Sec. II-C](#S2.SS3 "II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries").

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by
quality at saturation
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
the task structure leaving quantity slack. A rollout is a single
decoding pass over a static input, an episode with $`T\!=\!1`$ except
where tool calls precede the answer \[[216](#bib.bib98),
[232](#bib.bib270), [228](#bib.bib277), [225](#bib.bib286),
[220](#bib.bib284), [224](#bib.bib271)\], and leaves no side effect to
revert, keeping both interaction cost and recoverability from lowering
$`\bar{K}`$. Information gain, in contrast, arises in single-answer
episodes only from goals whose pass rate under the current solver lies
strictly between zero and one. A dataset or a fixed generator bounds the
supply of such goals by how many lie near the edge of the current
agent’s competence, a number that depends on the backbone’s pretraining
and, by the mechanism that stalls self-play \[[131](#bib.bib56)\],
shrinks as the agent masters these goals.

Self-Posed Goals.   Larger groups do not appear to substitute for
informative goals under self-consistency rewards, which lose contrast as
groups grow, and loops raise the information gain instead by letting the
agent pose its goals or by reweighting goals by pass rate, at a cost
paid in feedback. Reported group sizes stay between four and ten
rollouts per goal despite cheap decoding passes \[[7](#bib.bib46),
[216](#bib.bib98), [6](#bib.bib48), [22](#bib.bib43), [8](#bib.bib47),
[218](#bib.bib54), [234](#bib.bib211), [126](#bib.bib212),
[127](#bib.bib213), [232](#bib.bib270), [215](#bib.bib273)\], and EvoLMM
finds its self-consistency reward best at four to six samples, reporting
over-consensus collapse at twelve \[[22](#bib.bib43)\], consistent with
the reward, not the cost, limiting $`K_{k}`$. The agent enters
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ either as a generative role within $`\Phi_{\theta}`$
that synthesizes the question beside the solver, and in some loops the
visual input, or through a rule that reweights dataset or generator
goals by the solver’s pass rate, alone in
SyncLoop \[[208](#bib.bib278)\] or on top of a learned
proposer \[[237](#bib.bib275), [239](#bib.bib280), [209](#bib.bib281)\].
Proposer-solver loops after R-Zero \[[243](#bib.bib133)\] reward goals
of intermediate solver agreement through terms that vanish with
$`p_{g}(1-p_{g})`$ \[[234](#bib.bib211), [126](#bib.bib212)\], adding
diversity terms against a narrowing of goals \[[127](#bib.bib213),
[5](#bib.bib45)\]. These rewards are computed in FA yet reshape the goal
distribution of EG. In VisPlay, a trained Questioner lifts Qwen2.5-VL-3B
from 30.61 to 44.16 after one round against 33.77 for an untrained
Challenger \[[5](#bib.bib45)\], a comparison that attributes about three
quarters of the gain to learning the role. The gain is paid in feedback,
where a self-posed question lacks a key unless a program computes its
answer, leaving the answer to the agent’s own outputs.

### IV-B FA Bound by Realized Fidelity

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition groups of short answers to the
same question, or the tool-calling episodes of a frozen agent, and the
loops score each answer against one or more of three references
([Table VII](#S4.T7 "In IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning")).
The agent’s own outputs (a), through a majority vote, a self-judgment,
the proposer’s answer, or consistency under image transformations, score
self-posed or unlabeled questions \[[22](#bib.bib43), [5](#bib.bib45),
[23](#bib.bib127)\]. An answer computed by task generation (e) scores
questions whose answers programs, game rules, a geometric environment,
or a physics engine determine \[[64](#bib.bib176), [218](#bib.bib54),
[235](#bib.bib214), [239](#bib.bib280)\], and a pre-collected key (b)
scores labeled sets \[[221](#bib.bib129), [223](#bib.bib247),
[225](#bib.bib286)\]. Weight-updating methods mostly turn scores into
group-normalized rewards for GRPO-style updates or into preference pairs
for DPO \[[7](#bib.bib46), [5](#bib.bib45), [213](#bib.bib131),
[214](#bib.bib276)\], whereas training-free methods use them to admit
skills, tools, or notes into a library \[[146](#bib.bib175),
[225](#bib.bib286), [222](#bib.bib285)\].

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound
by realized fidelity
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
its attainable fidelity being high and localization imposing little. A
short answer admits exact match against a reference fixed outside the
agent and leaves no channel unchecked, and without a key the
program-computed answers of VQS stay correct on 94.4% of retained
questions among 500 human-audited ones \[[64](#bib.bib176)\], a lower
bound on $`\bar{F}`$ under the conversion of
[Sec. III-C](#S3.SS3 "III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop").
Consensus already falls below this bound within one round, with 24% of
retained majority-vote labels and 18% of retained model-judge labels
wrong in the same audit \[[64](#bib.bib176)\]. Across rounds, externally
estimated pseudo-label accuracy falls from 72.0 to 61.0 over three
iterations in VisPlay \[[5](#bib.bib45)\] and from 64.5 to 37.5 over
five in Video-Zero \[[160](#bib.bib204)\], declines that bear on
$`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ only jointly with rising question difficulty, to which
VisPlay attributes its own. Gaming resistance of the vote under long
optimization remains untested here, whereas prolonged training against a
majority-vote self-reward in text-only reasoning ends in reward hacking
and abrupt collapse \[[244](#bib.bib252)\]. Single-answer episodes fix
$`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$, the step-level agreement of iReasoner refining credit
only within the output \[[170](#bib.bib44)\], and only the short
tool-integrated episodes of Agent0-VL, scored as a
whole \[[216](#bib.bib98)\], leave credit coarser.

Vote Preconditions and Evaluator Drift.   With localization free, every
deficit of feedback acquisition is a fidelity deficit, and self-derived
rewards make that fidelity a property of the model being trained. A vote
recovers the model’s belief and tracks $`R`$ only where answers admit an
equivalence relation and the pretrained prior concentrates on the
correct answer \[[80](#bib.bib96), [132](#bib.bib111)\], discrete
answers supplying the first condition and the backbone, not the task
structure, deciding the second. Within these conditions the reward form
matters, TTRV lowering accuracy on four of five VQA benchmarks under a
hard majority-vote reward and raising it on all five under a
frequency-proportional reward with entropy
control \[[171](#bib.bib209)\]. The evaluators further differ in whether
they move with the policy: votes over current samples, parameter-sharing
supervisors \[[126](#bib.bib212)\], and self-judging
models \[[214](#bib.bib276)\] keep the agent edge into FA, judges frozen
at the initial model cut it \[[212](#bib.bib128), [230](#bib.bib177)\],
and the moving-average verifier of Trinity lags the policy by
construction \[[231](#bib.bib215)\]. A frozen evaluator still shares the
prior of the policies descended from it, removing drift but not a fixed
bias, and reports under differing numbers of rounds leave the designs
uncompared. Answers fixed outside the agent, by a key or a program,
restore $`\bar{F}`$ only for labeled sets and program-computable
families, the same restriction that experience generation imposes on the
goals.

### IV-C UC Bound by Retention

Update consolidation in multimodal reasoning persists the scored
experience in two forms, weight updates and training-free writes
([Table VII](#S4.T7 "In IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning")).
Weight-updating methods write $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ with an update rule
fixed before the loop, through group-relative policy gradients,
preference optimization, or fine-tuning, either once per round over two
to nine reported rounds \[[5](#bib.bib45), [160](#bib.bib204),
[64](#bib.bib176), [235](#bib.bib214), [238](#bib.bib245),
[209](#bib.bib281), [214](#bib.bib276)\] or continuously within a single
training run. Training-free methods keep a frozen VLM and let the agent
write text or code into skill and tool libraries \[[146](#bib.bib175),
[223](#bib.bib247), [225](#bib.bib286), [220](#bib.bib284),
[227](#bib.bib282)\], memory cards or notes \[[219](#bib.bib246),
[222](#bib.bib285), [226](#bib.bib279)\], or harnesses of tools, skills,
and execution code \[[224](#bib.bib271), [233](#bib.bib283)\], over
benchmark streams or, in VisualEvolve, up to sixteen rounds, whereas a
separate o4-mini abstracts the tool library of
TVP \[[217](#bib.bib274)\]. MetaForge alone combines the two,
registering validated tools that its policy forges during GRPO into a
persistent library \[[228](#bib.bib277)\].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is
bound by retention
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
inferred from non-monotone curves, not a measured loss, whereas
generalization, though reported, is confounded with the backbone prior.
No method measures retention on earlier-round goals, and the closest
evidence, per-round scores on a fixed benchmark suite, traces the
increment $`\mathcal{J}_{k+1}-\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ of
[Eq. 6](#S2.E6 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries")
over the evaluation distribution, not the trained goals. These curves
rise monotonically in Agent0-VL \[[216](#bib.bib98)\] but peak or dip
mid-run elsewhere \[[8](#bib.bib47), [5](#bib.bib45)\], while single
benchmarks reverse more often, MM-Vet falling from 48.62 to 38.07 over
three VisPlay iterations as the average rises \[[5](#bib.bib45)\]. Among
weight-updating methods, only ISR-DPO and Marvo run beyond five rounds,
the former gaining through its ninth iteration \[[214](#bib.bib276)\]
and the latter degrading after about the fifth or sixth of
eight \[[232](#bib.bib270)\]. Parametric writes generalize more freely,
reaching any goal that activates the updated weights and lifting
standard benchmarks after training on synthesized
questions \[[7](#bib.bib46), [5](#bib.bib45), [22](#bib.bib43)\]. These
gains are consistent with elicitation of the backbone prior, most
weight-updating methods resting on Qwen2.5-VL or Qwen3-VL, the family
whose text-only counterparts gain even under spurious
rewards \[[204](#bib.bib251)\]. V-Zero offers a partial control,
reaching 51.9 against 50.8 for supervised GRPO on the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B
backbone \[[7](#bib.bib46)\], and only an equal-budget non-evolving
baseline would separate self-evolution from elicitation. Non-parametric
writes act only when retrieved, and their transfer is tested directly,
EvoSpatial evaluating libraries frozen after one benchmark on 18
others \[[220](#bib.bib284)\] and VideoEvoHarness moving an evolved
harness to a second backbone \[[233](#bib.bib283)\].

Reference-Gated Writes.   Consolidation inherits its exposure from the
first two stages, and the two forms of writing differ in how they guard
against it. Where the evaluator moves with the policy or a proposer
supplies the goals, a parametric write is scored and driven by
quantities that change with the update itself, and the update rule
accepts every scored step without a fixed reference that could reveal a
later round erasing an earlier gain. Several training-free methods gate
their writes against such a reference, admitting a skill or change only
on a validation or held-out gain \[[146](#bib.bib175),
[233](#bib.bib283)\], promoting a skill-tool pair only on a strict gain
over its training sample \[[225](#bib.bib286)\], rolling back note edits
that do not raise batch accuracy \[[222](#bib.bib285)\], or selecting
snapshots on fixed validation or development sets \[[223](#bib.bib247),
[224](#bib.bib271)\], whereas TVP checks a new tool only against the
outputs of the programs it replaces \[[217](#bib.bib274)\]. A guard on
retention thus exists only where gated training-free writes keep a fixed
reference.

### IV-D Limits and Preconditions

Bottleneck Attribution.   The binding bottlenecks of feedback and
consolidation arise from self-reference, not from task structure. Both
ceilings are slack for any learning loop, and a fixed loop that trains
against pre-collected keys, as M-STAR does \[[152](#bib.bib49)\], scores
its rollouts at the fidelity of an exact match. The weight-updating
branch gives up this reference to pose and answer its own questions, its
answers coming from the agent’s own outputs, whose realized fidelity
falls below $`\bar{F}`$, and its parametric writes lacking a fixed
reference against which a later round could be checked. The
training-free branch keeps the key or a validation set and admits
self-reference only through the update, shifting the cost to the writer,
whose frozen backbone both diagnoses a bottleneck and writes its remedy,
its capability bounding both, a limitation that Dynamo reports for
itself \[[225](#bib.bib286)\]. Self-reference repays part of this cost
in experience generation, where a learned proposer relieves the
saturation of fixed goal supplies and accounts for most of the
first-round gain of VisPlay \[[5](#bib.bib45)\]. The few cross-round
audits report declines confounded with rising question difficulty, and a
large question-answering prior in the backbones may account for part of
the gains in both branches, disqualifying the least constrained cell as
a clean baseline for the other scenarios. This attribution rests on the
stage evidence and on the provenance of each method in
[Table VII](#S4.T7 "In IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning"), not
on a controlled comparison with fixed loops.

Cross-Cycle Degradation.   Across cycles, self-reference exposes
multimodal reasoning to degradations that a fixed loop with keys avoids.
On the goal side, learned proposers extend the agent edge into
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ and pass-rate curricula open the goal
edge \[[208](#bib.bib278), [237](#bib.bib275), [239](#bib.bib280),
[209](#bib.bib281)\], both inviting curriculum collapse. On the feedback
side, self-derived rewards extend the agent edge into FA, inviting
compounding reward hacking, and training on self-labeled answers invites
model collapse along the edge into the rollout policy. The extension of
training-free writers into UC remains untested, and cross-round evidence
reduces to the Vision-Zero plateau, where a self-derived signal stops
informing updates \[[218](#bib.bib54)\], and the late-round decline of
Marvo \[[232](#bib.bib270)\], with per-round reversals of single
benchmarks fitting hacking and forgetting alike.

Presupposed Resources.   The mechanisms of multimodal reasoning
presuppose resources that its short, discrete answers supply. Majority
votes and agreement-based proposer rewards presuppose answers that admit
an equivalence relation \[[22](#bib.bib43), [234](#bib.bib211),
[126](#bib.bib212)\], program-computed answers presuppose a program that
determines the answer at task generation \[[64](#bib.bib176)\], and
reference-gated writes presuppose a key or validation set held outside
the writer \[[146](#bib.bib175), [225](#bib.bib286)\].

## V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation

Multimodal generation occupies the quadrant of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
in which only the fidelity ceiling is low, an open-ended image or video
having no reference output to be checked against outside sub-families
such as object counts, rendered text, or program-drawn charts. Training
against learned preference scorers fixed before the loop forms a fixed
loop that this ceiling already binds, such scorers being exploitable
under optimization \[[245](#bib.bib172), [129](#bib.bib165)\].
Weight-updating loops mostly derive the verifier from the agent, leaving
the ceiling unchanged but letting the verifier’s bias move with the
policy and exposing the loop to compounding reward hacking.
Training-free loops mostly let a frozen backbone judge its own outputs
and write its memory or skills, sharing one bias between judge and
writer. Reported loops run within one training run, over at most five
rounds, or over one pass of a task stream.

### V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts

In multimodal generation, experience generation draws prompts as goals,
paired with a source image in editing, and the outputs are images,
videos, 3D scenes, charts, diagrams, or educational animations. The task
families center on compositional text-to-image
prompts \[[128](#bib.bib39), [12](#bib.bib99), [11](#bib.bib163)\],
extending to aesthetic prompt optimization \[[246](#bib.bib164),
[247](#bib.bib168)\], text rendering \[[245](#bib.bib172)\],
safety \[[248](#bib.bib219)\], charts \[[191](#bib.bib216)\],
text-to-video generation \[[249](#bib.bib289), [250](#bib.bib292)\],
image editing \[[251](#bib.bib288), [252](#bib.bib290)\], and diagrams,
3D scenes, method illustrations, and animations built through tool
chains \[[253](#bib.bib226), [254](#bib.bib224), [255](#bib.bib227),
[256](#bib.bib170)\]. These goals come from a fixed pool or from
generative roles of the agent, and weight-updating loops sample
$`K_{k}`$ outputs per prompt in one pass each, whereas training-free
loops run a frozen agent through a workflow of tool calls, renders, and
edits.
[Table IX](#S5.T9 "In V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts ‣ V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation")
summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of
[Sec. II-C](#S2.SS3 "II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries").

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by
quality at the coverage of checkable prompts
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
the task structure leaving quantity slack. A rollout costs one sampling
pass or an offline tool chain \[[103](#bib.bib225)\] and leaves no side
effect to revert, with reported group sizes of three to sixteen samples
per prompt \[[128](#bib.bib39), [129](#bib.bib165), [13](#bib.bib417),
[9](#bib.bib63), [257](#bib.bib167), [245](#bib.bib172)\]. Information
gain, in contrast, runs out at the edge of what a check can score, not
at the edge of the agent’s competence as in multimodal reasoning. Fixed
pools come from benchmark categories whose attributes a detector, OCR,
or a VQA model scores, such as those of GenEval and
T2I-CompBench \[[128](#bib.bib39), [129](#bib.bib165),
[11](#bib.bib163), [10](#bib.bib38)\], and a learning loop drives pass
rates on such a pool toward one, where $`p_{g}(1-p_{g})`$ approaches
zero, as the fixed loop Flow-GRPO raises SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95 on
GenEval \[[195](#bib.bib173)\]. Open-ended prompts would still separate
good outputs from poor ones under $`R`$, yet no check fixed before the
loop scores them, leaving the loop unable to draw information from them.
Loops drawing every round from one prompt distribution report
diminishing gains by about the third round, consistent with this
saturation \[[12](#bib.bib99), [248](#bib.bib219)\].

Checkable Goal Composition.   A larger group adds samples of a prompt
without extending the checkable pool, and loops raise
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ instead by letting the agent compose
or reselect goals, at a cost paid in fidelity once the goals leave what
a fixed check scores. Built-in checks keep composed goals within
checkable sub-families, fixing answers at prompt construction in
UniRL \[[128](#bib.bib39)\], decomposing each prompt into yes/no
questions in SILMM \[[12](#bib.bib99)\], and restricting the
specifications that RSI in UMMs plans from its own failures to charts
that program execution verifies \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. Goals beyond
these sub-families fall to frozen external judges \[[258](#bib.bib220),
[259](#bib.bib208), [260](#bib.bib218)\], whereas ASG poses
understanding questions over unlabeled images, scored by the agreement
of its own answers across framings at a fidelity that moves with the
policy \[[40](#bib.bib166)\], and reselection stays within the pool,
InternalGap regenerating the prompts that yielded no accepted
image \[[11](#bib.bib163)\]. Controlled returns are reported only for
built-in checks and external judges, RSI in UMMs reaching 59.0% on
charts after four rounds against 46.3% for longer training on its
original data and leading a fixed distribution of equally many verified
charts in every round \[[191](#bib.bib216)\], and RSIgen gaining 4.7,
3.1, and 2.2 points over curricula compiled from frozen sources across
its three attempts \[[260](#bib.bib218)\].

### V-B FA Bound by Attainable Fidelity

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition a group of outputs for the same
prompt or the renders of one workflow, and the loops score each output
as a whole
([Table IX](#S5.T9 "In V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts ‣ V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation")).
The scores come from the agent itself (a), through the generator’s
confidence, its understanding branch, a lagged, snapshot, or co-trained
judge, or the frozen backbone that runs the workflow, or from outside
it, through an external judge (b) or program execution (e).
Weight-updating methods mostly turn scores into group-normalized rewards
for GRPO-style updates or into preference pairs for
DPO \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165), [13](#bib.bib417),
[12](#bib.bib99), [246](#bib.bib164)\], whereas training-free methods
receive verbal critiques, checklist scores, or pass/fail
verdicts \[[254](#bib.bib224), [253](#bib.bib226), [264](#bib.bib221),
[103](#bib.bib225)\] that trigger repairs within an episode and gate
persistent writes.

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound
by the fidelity ceiling
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
to which signal source, channel coverage, and gaming resistance each
contribute, while localization imposes little. An image admits no
equivalence check against a fixed reference, leaving learned scorers and
model judges, whose agreement with humans on open-ended content can turn
negative, the frozen reviewer of ManimAgent correlating with blind
ratings of 37 educational videos at
$`r\!=\!-0.17`$ \[[256](#bib.bib170)\]. Instruments fixed before the
loop score parts of the objective, such as detectors, OCR, and PickScore
in Flow-GRPO \[[195](#bib.bib173)\] and HPS-v2.1, CLIP, and VideoAlign
in DanceGRPO \[[267](#bib.bib174)\], and Flow-GRPO raises PickScore and
OCR accuracy while human raters judge its images below the base model in
quality \[[245](#bib.bib172)\]. Under optimization, IRIS attributes the
realism drop of its HPSv2-trained baseline to reward
hacking \[[129](#bib.bib165)\]. Only sub-families with a closed-form
predicate escape the ceiling, RSI in UMMs gaining more on charts from
execution-verified data than from the model’s own best-rated
images \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. Localization stays near
$`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$, a single sampling pass forming one action and
tool-orchestrated systems scoring renders with execution errors as their
chief step-level signal \[[256](#bib.bib170), [103](#bib.bib225)\].

Verifier Dependence on the Policy.   With localization nearly free,
every deficit of feedback acquisition is a fidelity deficit, and the
methods differ in how far the verifier depends on the policy it scores.
A verifier that depends on the current policy keeps the agent edge into
FA, letting $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ move with each update and inviting
compounding reward hacking, whereas weaker dependence slows or cuts that
edge and leaves a bias fixed across cycles. Generator confidence depends
on the policy entirely, and SOLACE and IRIS disagree even on its sign,
rewarding higher denoising confidence and lower self-certainty,
respectively \[[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165)\].
Understanding-branch checks hold only the prompt fixed and substitute
for an external verifier only if the judging parameters are separated
from the judged ones, the two directions are symmetric, and
understanding exceeds generation. Shared weights violate the first
condition, which KL penalties to a reference policy slow but do not
remove \[[10](#bib.bib38), [128](#bib.bib39), [40](#bib.bib166),
[13](#bib.bib417)\], the non-inverse relation between text-to-image and
image-to-text weakens the second behind reverse-likelihood
rewards \[[10](#bib.bib38), [257](#bib.bib167), [261](#bib.bib287)\],
and the third, the internal gap that InternalGap converts into
supervision \[[11](#bib.bib163)\], remains untested within a
run \[[10](#bib.bib38)\]. Weaker dependence comes from co-evolving or
lagged verifiers \[[246](#bib.bib164), [263](#bib.bib291),
[245](#bib.bib172), [249](#bib.bib289), [262](#bib.bib217)\], from
frozen self-verifiers \[[247](#bib.bib168), [251](#bib.bib288)\],
including frozen backbones that also write the
update \[[256](#bib.bib170), [264](#bib.bib221), [254](#bib.bib224)\],
and from external or programmatic verifiers \[[259](#bib.bib208),
[260](#bib.bib218), [191](#bib.bib216)\], and no report compares these
designs at a matched number of rounds. Such designs thus trade a moving
bias for a fixed one without raising $`\bar{F}`$.

### V-C UC Bound by Retention

Update consolidation in multimodal generation persists the scored
experience in two forms, weight updates and training-free writes
([Table IX](#S5.T9 "In V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts ‣ V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation")).
Weight-updating methods write $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ with an update rule
fixed before the loop, through group-relative policy gradients,
preference optimization, fine-tuning, or self-distillation, either
continuously within a single training run or over two to five reported
rounds \[[246](#bib.bib164), [247](#bib.bib168), [12](#bib.bib99),
[249](#bib.bib289), [191](#bib.bib216), [248](#bib.bib219)\].
Training-free methods keep the generator and the agent frozen and let
the agent write memory \[[256](#bib.bib170), [265](#bib.bib171),
[165](#bib.bib222), [253](#bib.bib226), [250](#bib.bib292)\], skill,
constraint-function, concept, or middleware
libraries \[[264](#bib.bib221), [254](#bib.bib224), [103](#bib.bib225),
[255](#bib.bib227)\], or routing records \[[258](#bib.bib220)\], over a
task stream or up to five rounds. ImageRSI alone combines the two,
admitting experience to a library while retraining its judge and not its
generator \[[262](#bib.bib217)\].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is
bound by retention
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
documented within runs and in RSI in UMMs over at most four rounds,
whereas generalization is mostly untested and not shown to fail. Only
RSI in UMMs measures retention on earlier-round goals, exact category
text on an earlier vocabulary falling from 72% to 60% once a round
replaces that vocabulary and recovering when later rounds keep half of
the old specifications, while general understanding, which the chart
goals do not exercise, erodes by 2.6 points on
MMBench \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. Within single runs, iteration robustness
fails at the grain of optimizer steps, SOLACE degenerating into
textureless images under prolonged optimization \[[9](#bib.bib63)\] and
IRIS into meaningless images within hundreds of
steps \[[129](#bib.bib165)\], and across rounds, per-round scores cannot
separate saturation from erosion, as in the slight slip of DreamLLM
under SILMM on DPG-Bench \[[12](#bib.bib99)\]. Generalization is tested
only where a loop holds out evaluation goals \[[129](#bib.bib165),
[262](#bib.bib217), [253](#bib.bib226)\], which MemoGen does
not \[[265](#bib.bib171)\], and transfer is partial for both forms of
writing, a memory that SIDiffAgent builds on GenAI-Bench raising
DrawBench from 0.860 to 0.873 against 0.901 for in-domain
memory \[[165](#bib.bib222)\] and the parametric writes of RSI in UMMs
gaining only from 11.0% to 11.9% on a chart subset its authors judge too
hard for open models \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. Understanding-branch gains
also remain entangled with the prior that judge and generator share in a
unified model.

Self-Judged Writes.   The exposure that consolidation faces comes from
feedback acquisition, where the agent itself judges most writes, and the
two forms of writing guard against it differently. Where the verifier
depends on the policy, a parametric write is scored by the policy itself
or by a judge that follows it, and the update rule admits every rewarded
step, held back only by regularizers such as KL
penalties \[[10](#bib.bib38), [128](#bib.bib39), [40](#bib.bib166),
[9](#bib.bib63), [129](#bib.bib165), [13](#bib.bib417)\]. Training-free
writes pass an admission test before they persist, yet the reviewer
gating of ManimAgent \[[256](#bib.bib170)\] and the no-loss check of
COMFYCLAW on three held-out prompts that the agent
synthesizes \[[264](#bib.bib221)\] reuse the frozen model that judged
the experience, protecting retention on that model’s scale but not
against its bias. Only ImageRSI, through paired validation on separate
calibration and holdout splits \[[262](#bib.bib217)\], and Drawing
Middleware Evolution, through rollback against reference
illustrations \[[255](#bib.bib227)\], test writes outside that model.
Retention is thus protected only where a training-free write is tested
outside the model that judged it, a condition that the key- or
validation-gated writes of multimodal reasoning meet more often.

### V-D Limits and Preconditions

Bottleneck Attribution.   In multimodal generation, the fidelity ceiling
binds before self-reference, which changes the form of the deficit and
leaves the ceiling in place. The fixed loops of the scenario,
Flow-GRPO \[[195](#bib.bib173)\] and DanceGRPO \[[267](#bib.bib174)\]
among them, already train against exploitable
proxies \[[129](#bib.bib165)\], unlike the key-scored fixed loops of
multimodal reasoning \[[152](#bib.bib49)\]. Weight-updating loops
replace a proxy whose bias stays put with a policy-dependent verifier
whose bias moves with the policy \[[9](#bib.bib63),
[129](#bib.bib165)\], and training-free loops let the frozen model that
judges an output also write the update, judge and writer sharing one
bias. Goal selection is where self-reference earns back part of this
cost, controlled returns being reported there, whereas The Image as Its
Own Reward offers the only comparison of a moving verifier with a fixed
one, by human preference after one run \[[245](#bib.bib172)\]. Both the
ceiling and its cost rest on stage evidence and the provenance in
[Table IX](#S5.T9 "In V-A EG Bound by Checkable Prompts ‣ V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation"),
not on a controlled comparison.

Cross-Cycle Degradation.   Across cycles, self-reference opens paths
along which degradation follows the agent, with only one degradation
measured across rounds. On the goal side, learned proposers extend the
agent edge into $`\sigma_{\omega}`$, and the regeneration of failed
prompts in InternalGap \[[11](#bib.bib163)\] and the pruning of prompts
by pass rate in OctoT2I \[[258](#bib.bib220)\] open the goal edge, both
inviting curriculum collapse. The goal edge also carries this one
measured degradation, the forgetting in RSI in UMMs following a
vocabulary change that a rule reading the agent’s OCR score
triggers \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. On the feedback side, self-verifiers
extend the agent edge into FA, inviting compounding reward hacking,
observed only within single runs \[[9](#bib.bib63),
[129](#bib.bib165)\], and training on self-generated images invites
model collapse, which the narrowing of IRIS outputs under higher image
self-certainty resembles without isolating \[[129](#bib.bib165)\].
Curriculum collapse, the extension into UC, and cross-round
self-verifier fidelity remain untested.

Presupposed Resources.   The mechanisms of multimodal generation
presuppose resources that only part of its outputs supply.
Understanding-branch checks presuppose an output that the agent’s own
perception can process and an understanding branch stronger than its
generation \[[10](#bib.bib38), [11](#bib.bib163)\], built-in checks and
execution-verified goals presuppose a sub-family with a closed-form
predicate \[[128](#bib.bib39), [191](#bib.bib216)\], and admission gates
presuppose held-out splits or reference sets outside the judging
model \[[262](#bib.bib217), [255](#bib.bib227)\].

## VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation

GUI and Web navigation occupies the quadrant of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
in which only the quantity ceiling is low, each rollout being a
multi-step episode that pays environment latency at every step, whereas
the inspectable end state of an application or a web page keeps the
attainable fidelity high in sandboxed environments, where per-task
scripts read it. Much automated online learning here runs as fixed
loops, whose tasks and verifiers come from external models or benchmark
authors and never read the agent’s record \[[101](#bib.bib134),
[130](#bib.bib101), [200](#bib.bib140), [268](#bib.bib138),
[269](#bib.bib148), [270](#bib.bib390), [271](#bib.bib391),
[272](#bib.bib392), [273](#bib.bib393), [274](#bib.bib394),
[275](#bib.bib395), [276](#bib.bib396), [277](#bib.bib397)\].
Weight-updating loops allocate scarce rollouts by proposing goals or
reweighting a fixed task set by its success record, and buy step-level
credit with verifiers refit on the agent’s trajectories, whose fidelity
moves with the policy. Training-free loops keep the task set fixed and
reuse each episode through memory or skills that a frozen backbone
writes and judges, sharing one bias between judge and writer. Reported
loops span one training run, a few rounds, or one pass over a task
stream, mostly evaluated on the task sets they train on.

### VI-A EG Bound by Rollout Cost

In GUI and Web navigation, experience generation draws goals that pair a
natural-language instruction with the initial state of an application,
desktop, or website, and each rollout is an episode of screenshots,
often with an accessibility tree, and actions such as taps, typing, and
scrolls, ending in success, failure, or a step limit. The task families
span mobile apps in AitW, AndroidWorld, and
AndroidLab \[[14](#bib.bib42), [17](#bib.bib293), [135](#bib.bib139)\],
desktop software in OSWorld \[[115](#bib.bib147), [16](#bib.bib135),
[278](#bib.bib294)\], and web navigation in WebArena and VisualWebArena
sandboxes and on live WebVoyager and Online-Mind2Web
sites \[[201](#bib.bib298), [284](#bib.bib297), [163](#bib.bib228)\].
These goals come from a benchmark task set, a task stream, or the
agent’s own proposals, and weight-updating loops run episode groups per
goal in parallel instances, whereas training-free loops run one or a few
episodes in sequence with a frozen backbone.
[Table XI](#S6.T11 "In VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation")
summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of
[Sec. II-C](#S2.SS3 "II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries").

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by
quantity at the episodes that parallel environment instances afford
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
an episode cost that the single passes of multimodal reasoning and
generation do not incur. A rollout spans up to 25 screen-action
steps \[[130](#bib.bib101)\], each paying rendering and environment
latency on top of policy inference, 2.5 to 4.0 seconds per step on the
virtual machines of UI-TARS-2 \[[125](#bib.bib144)\], with DART-GUI
reporting episodes that last tens of minutes \[[115](#bib.bib147)\].
Group sizes of eight to 64 rollouts per task \[[130](#bib.bib101),
[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293), [101](#bib.bib134)\] are bought
with parallel instances, up to 64 emulators in
DigiRL \[[14](#bib.bib42)\], whereas training-free loops run each task
once or a few times in sequence \[[162](#bib.bib137),
[163](#bib.bib228), [280](#bib.bib295), [281](#bib.bib145)\]. Quality
decides what each scarce episode returns, and on long-horizon tasks the
loss falls mostly on goals beyond the agent’s reach, where a binary
outcome gives $`p_{g}(1-p_{g})\approx 0`$, consistent with starting
success rates of 11.3% on the professional software of
SEAgent \[[16](#bib.bib135)\] and 18.1% on AndroidLab in
UI-Genie \[[135](#bib.bib139)\].

Reuse, Reweighting, and Goal Generation.   A larger group costs
environment instances, and loops raise
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ instead along three routes, reuse,
reweighting, and goal generation, which the inspectable end state keeps
verifiable. Under stationary sampling, reuse raises the return of later
episodes by conditioning them on memory and skills that the agent
writes \[[162](#bib.bib137), [278](#bib.bib294), [282](#bib.bib300),
[279](#bib.bib296), [280](#bib.bib295), [163](#bib.bib228),
[281](#bib.bib145), [283](#bib.bib362)\] or by training the agent on
steps that value functions or reward models fit on its rollouts select
and label \[[14](#bib.bib42), [144](#bib.bib143)\], both lifting
unreachable tasks toward informative success rates. Reweighting by the
success record keeps the verifier of a fixed task set, lowering the
rollout count of tasks with high running success in
DART-GUI \[[115](#bib.bib147)\] and the sampling probability of tasks
that earn no reward over consecutive epochs in
MobileRL \[[17](#bib.bib293)\], or returning earlier
failures \[[135](#bib.bib139)\]. Goal generation needs a verifier for
each new goal, which reads the outcome off the screen through a model or
judge fixed before the loop \[[16](#bib.bib135), [15](#bib.bib299)\] or
a check that the agent itself runs \[[284](#bib.bib297),
[201](#bib.bib298)\]. Each route carries a controlled return, and the
most direct test of substitution favors reuse, EvoSkill-GUI with skills
outperforming pass@3 without them on MobileWorld at a comparable token
budget \[[281](#bib.bib145)\], while removing the failure filter of
MobileRL lowers its AndroidWorld success \[[17](#bib.bib293)\] and
random task generation lowers ACuRL’s third-round LibreOffice Impress
score from 40.7% to 36.4% \[[15](#bib.bib299)\].

### VI-B FA Bound by Localization

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition an episode of screens and actions,
which most loops score once at its end and loops with learned step
judges score per step
([Table XI](#S6.T11 "In VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation")).
Scores from outside the agent (b) come from per-task scripts and
rule-based rewards written with the benchmark \[[115](#bib.bib147),
[17](#bib.bib293)\], the fixed evaluators of DigiRL and
SEAgent \[[14](#bib.bib42), [16](#bib.bib135)\], and benchmark
success \[[280](#bib.bib295)\]. Scores from the agent (a) come from
value functions and reward models fit on its
trajectories \[[14](#bib.bib42), [135](#bib.bib139),
[144](#bib.bib143)\], the Judger role of the base model that SCALE
fine-tunes in its other roles \[[284](#bib.bib297)\], and the frozen
backbone that acts and judges its own episode in training-free
loops \[[162](#bib.bib137), [278](#bib.bib294), [279](#bib.bib296),
[163](#bib.bib228), [281](#bib.bib145), [201](#bib.bib298)\].
Weight-updating methods turn scores into group-normalized advantages or
rejection-sampled training targets \[[115](#bib.bib147),
[17](#bib.bib293), [135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143)\], whereas
training-free methods turn them into success labels and diagnoses that
gate memory and skill writes \[[278](#bib.bib294), [281](#bib.bib145),
[163](#bib.bib228)\].

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound
by localization
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
the attainable fidelity being high wherever the goal fixes an end state,
though signal sources reach that ceiling unevenly. Task completion
resides in the final screen, application database, or file system, which
per-task scripts and rule-based rewards inspect
directly \[[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293)\], whereas model judges
fall short, EvoSkill-GUI’s same-backbone critic erring on 28 of 143
audited failures and passing at least four as
successes \[[281](#bib.bib145)\]. Free-form goals and live websites lack
scripts and fall to screenshot judges \[[101](#bib.bib134),
[200](#bib.bib140), [201](#bib.bib298)\], which see the screen but not
the backend state. Under optimization, ACuRL audits its judge against
on-policy trajectories over three rounds, with precision of 89.1% to
98.0% \[[15](#bib.bib299)\], whereas judge benchmarks score fixed
trajectories \[[285](#bib.bib192)\] or the downstream success of
policies trained on each judge \[[142](#bib.bib193)\]. Localization
binds every source alike, even an exact checker spreading one verdict
over episodes of up to 50 actions \[[281](#bib.bib145)\], with
$`L_{\nu}`$ falling as episodes lengthen. Loops recover step-level
signal at a credit-assignment cost through learned value functions and
judges \[[14](#bib.bib42), [16](#bib.bib135), [135](#bib.bib139),
[144](#bib.bib143)\] or a failure-diagnosing critic for training-free
revision \[[281](#bib.bib145)\], step-level advantages speeding DigiRL’s
learning by about 12% on its Web Shopping subset \[[14](#bib.bib42)\].

Localization Bought with Fidelity.   With end states checkable, feedback
acquisition falls short in localization and lacks checkers for free-form
goals, and loops open the agent edge into FA to buy either. A value
function or reward model refit on the agent’s trajectories follows the
policy, letting $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ move with each round and inviting
compounding reward hacking, exploited errors re-entering the data on
which it is refit \[[14](#bib.bib42), [135](#bib.bib139),
[144](#bib.bib143)\]. MagicGUI-RMS slows this edge with a GPT-4o reward
model that arbitrates its domain model \[[144](#bib.bib143)\], yet both
it and UI-Genie track their reward models only on fixed labeled sets,
excluding the on-policy rollouts where exploitation would
surface \[[135](#bib.bib139)\]. A frozen self-judge keeps its bias fixed
but shares it with the writer \[[162](#bib.bib137), [278](#bib.bib294),
[279](#bib.bib296), [281](#bib.bib145), [201](#bib.bib298)\], its errors
cutting revision short, as the over-optimistic EvoSkill-GUI critic
shows. Verifiers fixed before the loop cut the edge, at the episode
level in DART-GUI and MobileRL \[[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293)\]
and at the step level in SEAgent’s World State
Model \[[16](#bib.bib135)\], which localizes credit independently of the
agent but exposes the loop to distribution shift once rollouts leave its
training distribution. Localization and free-form goal coverage thus
cost either fidelity that follows the agent or, from a model fixed
before the loop, distribution shift.

### VI-C UC Bound by Generalization

Update consolidation in GUI and Web navigation persists the scored
experience in two forms, weight updates and training-free writes, each
method using one of them
([Table XI](#S6.T11 "In VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation")).
Weight-updating methods write $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ with an update rule
fixed before the loop, either continuously within a single training
run \[[14](#bib.bib42), [115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293)\] or over
two or three rounds through GRPO with adversarial imitation,
reinforcement learning on generated tasks, or fine-tuning of the agent
and its reward model \[[16](#bib.bib135), [15](#bib.bib299),
[144](#bib.bib143), [135](#bib.bib139)\], while SCALE fine-tunes its
Selector and Predictor over repeated exploration
rounds \[[284](#bib.bib297)\]. Training-free methods keep the backbone
frozen and let the acting model write narrative, episodic, procedural,
or grounding memory \[[278](#bib.bib294), [279](#bib.bib296),
[282](#bib.bib300)\], tips and executable
shortcuts \[[162](#bib.bib137), [280](#bib.bib295)\], or skill packages
and executable APIs \[[281](#bib.bib145), [201](#bib.bib298)\], over one
pass of a task stream, a few attempts per task, or a fixed budget of
practice iterations, whereas a separate condenser writes the memory of
WebCoach \[[163](#bib.bib228)\].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is
bound by generalization
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
documented within one platform and mostly on the task sets that produced
the experience, whereas general capability, where measured, holds. No
method measures retention on earlier-round goals, and the closest
evidence concerns general capability, ACuRL keeping or raising its
scores on untrained environments by 2 to 7 points \[[15](#bib.bib299)\].
Elsewhere, replay sustains iteration robustness \[[14](#bib.bib42),
[17](#bib.bib293)\], and per-round scores rise without a reported
reversal \[[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143), [284](#bib.bib297)\],
though non-monotonically in Mobile-Agent-E \[[162](#bib.bib137)\],
tracking $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ on the current evaluation set, not
$`S_{\zeta}`$. Training-free libraries evolve on their evaluation
tasks \[[281](#bib.bib145), [162](#bib.bib137), [163](#bib.bib228)\], as
in several fixed loops \[[187](#bib.bib136), [104](#bib.bib142),
[164](#bib.bib230)\], measuring adaptation to a known goal distribution.
Held-out applications show transfer within the platform, MagicGUI-RMS
gaining about as much on unseen apps as in
domain \[[144](#bib.bib143)\], whereas ACuRL reaches a new software
version or operating system only by training
there \[[15](#bib.bib299)\]. Zero-shot transfer across platforms appears
only in the fixed loop GUI-HARVEST, whose frozen harness, evolved on
OSWorld, adds 6.47 points for Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and 13.87 for GPT-5
on WindowsAgentArena \[[286](#bib.bib301)\]. Cross-form comparisons are
confounded by backbone, training-free loops mostly running frozen
proprietary models and weight-updating loops open ones.

Author Checks and Reader Dependence.   What a write carries into the
agent is fixed in feedback acquisition, and the two forms of writing
differ in what checks a write before it persists and, for non-parametric
writes, in who reads it afterward. Parametric writes pass on the
verifier’s score alone, carrying its exposure unchanged, compounding
hacking for agent-derived verifiers \[[14](#bib.bib42),
[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143), [284](#bib.bib297)\] and
distribution shift for SEAgent’s frozen World State
Model \[[16](#bib.bib135)\], while exact checkers leave little to
inherit \[[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293)\]. Non-parametric writes
pass an admission test that mostly reuses the author’s judgment,
EvoSkill-GUI and MobileSteward admitting skills and memories largely on
their own critics’ verdicts \[[281](#bib.bib145), [279](#bib.bib296)\],
whereas SkillWeaver unit-tests each synthesized API against execution
feedback, a check outside the writer \[[201](#bib.bib298)\].
Self-written skills can carry errors, such as the redundant or missing
taps in the generated shortcuts of
Mobile-Agent-E \[[162](#bib.bib137)\], unlike the key- or
validation-gated writes of multimodal reasoning. Once admitted, a
non-parametric write takes effect only when a later rollout reads it,
its gain depending on the reader, as the memory that a separate
condenser writes for WebCoach lowers Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 32.8% to 31.1%
yet raises Skywork-r1v3-38B from 47.3% to 61.4% \[[163](#bib.bib228)\].
A non-parametric write is thus checked mostly by its author and valued
by its reader.

### VI-D Limits and Preconditions

Bottleneck Attribution.   In GUI and Web navigation, the quantity
ceiling binds fixed and self-evolving loops alike, and self-reference
leaves it in place, its cost lying in what each entry point puts at
risk. Fixed loops pay the same episode cost, scaling to thousands of
virtual machines in ComputerRL \[[269](#bib.bib148)\], and already train
against signals fixed before the loop, the verification functions of
ComputerRL at high fidelity and, below it, the screen judges of
ZeroGUI \[[101](#bib.bib134)\] and MobileGUI-RL \[[130](#bib.bib101)\].
A success-conditioned rule over a task set with fixed checkers risks
little, only the allocation following the agent \[[17](#bib.bib293)\],
whereas generated goals move verification from fixed checkers to learned
or prompted judges \[[16](#bib.bib135), [15](#bib.bib299),
[284](#bib.bib297), [201](#bib.bib298)\], refit value functions and
reward models buy localization with a fidelity that moves with the
policy \[[14](#bib.bib42), [135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143)\], and
a frozen backbone that judges and writes carries one bias into both
roles \[[278](#bib.bib294), [281](#bib.bib145)\]. The higher return of
each scarce episode recovers part of these costs, controlled gains being
reported for reuse, reweighting, and goal generation. No controlled
comparison with fixed loops isolates these costs, which we read off the
stage evidence and the provenance in
[Table XI](#S6.T11 "In VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation").

Cross-Cycle Degradation.   Across cycles, self-reference opens paths
along which degradation follows the agent, and the environment path adds
a shift specific to the scenario. On the goal side, success-conditioned
rules and outcome-conditioned generators open the goal edge and
agent-realized proposers extend the agent edge into
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ \[[115](#bib.bib147), [17](#bib.bib293),
[135](#bib.bib139), [16](#bib.bib135), [15](#bib.bib299),
[284](#bib.bib297), [201](#bib.bib298)\], inviting curriculum collapse,
which MobileRL risks by design in removing persistently failing
tasks \[[17](#bib.bib293)\], and forgetting once the goal distribution
moves, which replay mitigates \[[14](#bib.bib42), [17](#bib.bib293)\].
On the feedback side, refit verifiers extend the agent edge into FA,
inviting compounding reward hacking untested beyond the two or three
reported rounds, and training on self-generated trajectories invites
model collapse \[[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143),
[284](#bib.bib297)\], whereas frozen self-judges share a fixed bias with
the writer and open no such path. The extension into UC carries
erroneous writes, which Mobile-Agent-E reports within a single
pass \[[162](#bib.bib137)\], and the environment path carries the drift
of live websites between cycles, independently of the
agent \[[200](#bib.bib140), [205](#bib.bib62)\].

Presupposed Resources.   The mechanisms of GUI and Web navigation
presuppose resources that its environments supply. Repeated attempts at
a goal, on which group sampling and reweighting rest, presuppose an
environment that resets to a known state \[[115](#bib.bib147),
[17](#bib.bib293)\], checkers and screen judges presuppose an end state
that a program or a model can inspect \[[115](#bib.bib147),
[16](#bib.bib135)\], and non-parametric reuse presupposes a reader able
to exploit what the agent writes \[[163](#bib.bib228)\].

## VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation

Embodied manipulation occupies the quadrant of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
in which both ceilings are low on hardware, each rollout costing robot
time, a reset, and wear, and each outcome checkable only by a per-task
classifier or a learned judge. Simulation relaxes both, where
reinforcement learning against simulator success already forms fixed
loops \[[62](#bib.bib161), [287](#bib.bib162), [288](#bib.bib398)\] and
most self-evolving loops close before any hardware evaluation. The
methods differ chiefly in feedback source: simulator predicates keep
fidelity, agent-derived verifiers densify feedback at the cost of an
agent-tied bias, and external judges buy fidelity with per-query
latency. Self-reference enters mostly through these verifiers in
weight-updating loops and through memory, skills, and code that a frozen
model writes and judges in training-free loops. Reported loops run at
most tens of rounds or a bounded practice budget, and hardware evidence
rests on eight to thirty evaluation trials per task.

### VII-A EG Bound by Physical Rollouts

In embodied manipulation, experience generation draws goals that pair a
language instruction with a scene, and each rollout is an episode of
camera observations and robot actions, emitted by a
vision-language-action policy or by programs that a language model
writes over perception and control primitives. The task families center
on tabletop and household manipulation in LIBERO and its variants,
ManiSkill, RoboCasa, RoboTwin, Robosuite, VIMA-Bench, and
VLABench \[[293](#bib.bib305), [295](#bib.bib159), [294](#bib.bib306),
[69](#bib.bib233), [300](#bib.bib103), [190](#bib.bib151)\], extending
to memory-dependent tasks in RoboMemArena \[[292](#bib.bib304)\] and
physical tasks on robot arms \[[19](#bib.bib149), [21](#bib.bib155),
[301](#bib.bib303), [305](#bib.bib157)\]. These goals come from a
benchmark suite, a library of scene-feasible tasks, or the agent’s own
proposals, and weight-updating loops run groups of episodes in parallel
simulators, training-free loops sequential attempts, and hardware loops
one episode at a time, with RoboEvolve imagining episodes inside a
learned video simulator \[[298](#bib.bib158)\].
[Table XII](#S7.T12 "In VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation")
summarizes the self-evolving methods that satisfy the conditions of
[Sec. II-C](#S2.SS3 "II-C Defining Conditions of Self-Evolving Loops ‣ II Preliminaries").

Quantity and Quality Constraints.   Experience generation is bound by
both factors on hardware and chiefly by quality in simulation
([Table III](#S3.T3 "In III-A Loop Decomposition ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).
On hardware, quantity binds through physical time, human support, and
scene recoverability, each real-world experiment of Self-Improving EFMs
running about 20 hours with human station resets \[[19](#bib.bib149)\]
and 6.58% of the 456 autonomous episodes of Find Something You Can’t Do
ending in a scene that only a human restores \[[21](#bib.bib155)\].
Simulation lifts this bound with parallel environments and group
sampling \[[62](#bib.bib161), [18](#bib.bib50), [306](#bib.bib94)\], and
where it also supplies a success predicate, reinforcement learning needs
no agent-derived verifier and appears chiefly in fixed
loops \[[287](#bib.bib162), [95](#bib.bib59), [161](#bib.bib60),
[307](#bib.bib399), [308](#bib.bib400)\]. Quality binds on both sides, a
long-horizon task beyond the policy’s reach returning
$`p_{g}(1-p_{g})\approx 0`$, and on hardware a persistent workspace
leaves only part of a task library feasible after each
episode \[[21](#bib.bib155)\], each unreachable or infeasible task
costing a full physical rollout.

Task Choice and World Models.   A larger group is affordable only in
simulation, which also supplies the success predicate, and loops pull
two other levers: task choice raises $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$
at a cost paid in verification, and a learned world model buys rollouts
at a cost paid in fidelity. Task choice stays within a library or its
edits, Find Something You Can’t Do sampling scene-feasible tasks of low
recent success \[[21](#bib.bib155)\] and Reflection-VLA simplifying
failing tasks through edited simulation
definitions \[[304](#bib.bib51)\]. Self-proposed practice extends this
choice \[[302](#bib.bib307), [20](#bib.bib231), [166](#bib.bib156)\] and
needs a check for each new goal, supplied by simulator predicates, by
validation seeds that a sealed judge grades in
SEAR \[[20](#bib.bib231)\], or by verifiers of the agent’s own model in
RATs \[[302](#bib.bib307)\]. Controlled returns are reported for both,
removing the performance-aware curriculum of Find Something You Can’t Do
markedly slowing its real-world improvement \[[21](#bib.bib155)\],
failure-ranked collection lowering the ManiSkill failure rate of
Policy-Level RSI below random collection \[[296](#bib.bib309)\], and
curious play lifting the RATs executor on LIBERO-PRO to 44.3% against
36.3% without play and 38.3% with random play \[[302](#bib.bib307)\]. A
learned world model makes rollouts cheap and recoverable but passes its
errors to feedback, as in RoboEvolve, which co-trains its planner with a
video simulator from unlabeled seed images \[[298](#bib.bib158)\], and
in World-VLA-Loop, which sets long-horizon suites aside once generated
video degrades beyond about 300 frames \[[24](#bib.bib154)\].

### VII-B FA Bound by Real-Robot Fidelity

Each cycle hands feedback acquisition an episode of camera frames and
actions, together with the simulator state in simulation, and
[Table XII](#S7.T12 "In VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation")
groups the methods by who supplies the feedback. Scores from the
environment (e) come from simulator predicates, execution errors, and
termination status \[[290](#bib.bib203), [294](#bib.bib306),
[293](#bib.bib305), [292](#bib.bib304), [296](#bib.bib309),
[297](#bib.bib360)\]. Scores from the agent (a) come from progress heads
and value models frozen before reinforcement
learning \[[19](#bib.bib149), [145](#bib.bib52), [299](#bib.bib310)\],
from a co-trained critic or a reward proxy refit on the policy’s
rollouts \[[298](#bib.bib158), [25](#bib.bib311)\], and from the frozen
model that acts and then judges its own trials \[[300](#bib.bib103),
[190](#bib.bib151), [20](#bib.bib231), [301](#bib.bib303),
[302](#bib.bib307), [303](#bib.bib361)\]. Scores from outside the agent
(b) come from VLM judges and critics \[[304](#bib.bib51),
[18](#bib.bib50), [69](#bib.bib233), [21](#bib.bib155),
[305](#bib.bib157)\]. Weight-updating methods turn scores into rewards
or advantages for on- or off-policy reinforcement
learning \[[18](#bib.bib50), [69](#bib.bib233), [19](#bib.bib149),
[145](#bib.bib52), [299](#bib.bib310)\], whereas training-free methods
turn them into success labels and diagnoses that gate memory, skill, and
code writes \[[300](#bib.bib103), [290](#bib.bib203),
[294](#bib.bib306)\].

Fidelity and Localization Constraints.   Feedback acquisition is bound
on real robots by fidelity and by a localization whose step-level
signals inherit the fidelity of their estimators
([Table IV](#S3.T4 "In III-B Stage 1: Experience Generation (EG) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
the attainable fidelity being high in simulation and low on hardware. A
simulator predicate checks completion exactly, whereas on a real robot a
judge must infer it from images with an accuracy reported between 69%
and 100% across judges and test sets, from 100% for the best of five VLM
judges on 100 image pairs in Find Something You Can’t
Do \[[21](#bib.bib155)\] to 78.9% for the judge of SOAR on 546
trajectories \[[173](#bib.bib160)\] and 69% to 75% for that of
VideoAgent on 36 videos \[[172](#bib.bib153)\]. Cameras show an
outcome’s appearance and not contact or force, which judges reading
images cannot observe. Under optimization, SEAR reports agents working
around its sealed judge, for instance by reading object geometry from
asset files \[[20](#bib.bib231)\], and policies trained against VLM
judges learn to exploit them \[[143](#bib.bib206)\]. Localization comes
only from learned estimators, such as progress heads, VLAC critics, and
per-step verifiers, which return a signal at every step or
sub-goal \[[19](#bib.bib149), [145](#bib.bib52), [69](#bib.bib233),
[302](#bib.bib307)\], whereas a simulator predicate or a real-robot
judge returns one verdict per episode.

Dense Feedback from Learned Verifiers.   A simulator predicate stays
fixed as the policy improves, whereas the learned verifiers that make
real-robot feedback dense or cheap incur degradations set by whether
they follow the policy. Progress heads and value models frozen before
reinforcement learning cut the agent edge \[[19](#bib.bib149),
[145](#bib.bib52), [299](#bib.bib310)\] but meet distribution shift on
states that the improving policy reaches outside its imitation data, the
key challenge Self-Improving EFMs names for its reward
model \[[19](#bib.bib149)\]. Co-trained critics keep the edge and invite
compounding reward hacking, which RoboEvolve counters by binarizing its
physical reward terms, citing as stability monotone reward curves that
hacking would equally produce \[[298](#bib.bib158)\], and MERL by
down-weighting low-trust imagined chunks, outperforming a matched
control \[[25](#bib.bib311)\]. A frozen self-judge opens no path into FA
but writes its misjudged trials into the memory or skills it later
retrieves \[[300](#bib.bib103), [190](#bib.bib151), [20](#bib.bib231),
[301](#bib.bib303), [302](#bib.bib307)\], unless a sealed judge checks
them on validation seeds, a judge that the agents of SEAR still
circumvent \[[20](#bib.bib231)\]. External judges stay independent of
the policy but cost 2.6 to 16.9 s per query in Find Something You Can’t
Do \[[21](#bib.bib155)\], bounding the rollouts they can score. Dense
feedback on hardware thus rests on fidelity audited within one task
distribution, for judges on at most a few hundred
samples \[[172](#bib.bib153), [21](#bib.bib155), [173](#bib.bib160)\]
and for the progress head on target-task
demonstrations \[[19](#bib.bib149)\].

### VII-C UC Bound by Generalization

Update consolidation in embodied manipulation persists the scored
experience in weight updates, training-free writes, or, in four methods,
both
([Table XII](#S7.T12 "In VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation")).
Weight-updating methods write $`\Phi_{\theta}`$ with an update rule
fixed before the loop, through reinforcement learning or fine-tuning on
their own successes, RoboEvolve updating its video simulator alongside
its planner \[[19](#bib.bib149), [304](#bib.bib51), [18](#bib.bib50),
[145](#bib.bib52), [21](#bib.bib155), [296](#bib.bib309),
[299](#bib.bib310), [25](#bib.bib311), [298](#bib.bib158)\].
Training-free methods keep the backbone frozen and let the agent’s
language model write reflections \[[300](#bib.bib103),
[301](#bib.bib303)\], skills, code, or harnesses \[[290](#bib.bib203),
[20](#bib.bib231), [294](#bib.bib306), [302](#bib.bib307),
[303](#bib.bib361), [190](#bib.bib151), [289](#bib.bib202),
[297](#bib.bib360)\], or memory of verified behaviors and physical
knowledge \[[292](#bib.bib304), [293](#bib.bib305),
[291](#bib.bib232)\], over two to 50 rounds, a rollout budget, or one
pass of a task stream. ViSkill \[[295](#bib.bib159)\],
Agentic-VLA \[[69](#bib.bib233)\], and Robo-COP \[[305](#bib.bib157)\]
train the policy alongside skill cards, a memory of adapted weights, or
admitted skills, and EmbodiedRSI keeps its VLA frozen while training the
policy that manages its memory of code and
skills \[[166](#bib.bib156)\].

Retention and Generalization Constraints.   Update consolidation is
bound by generalization
([Table V](#S3.T5 "In III-C Stage 2: Feedback Acquisition (FA) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")),
success falling with the distance of the test from practice even where
gains persist within one benchmark, whereas retention is measured only
in fixed loops, self-evolving ones guarding against regression by gates.
The code policies of SEAR fall from 87.8% on new initial states of
practiced tasks to 33.3% on new tasks and 28.7% under a new simulator
and action interface, and its trained VLAs from 73.2% to 43.1% and
10.2% \[[20](#bib.bib231)\]. Gains of written artifacts persist within
one benchmark, SHAPER adding 2.5 points on its in-domain VLABench split
and 6.0 to 10.0 on splits with unseen targets or task
forms \[[190](#bib.bib151)\], although its absolute success on the
splits with unseen targets falls from 42.5% to 26.0% and 19.5%. Hardware
transfer is tested on small sets, five tasks of 30 trials each in
EmbodiedRSI \[[166](#bib.bib156)\], eight scenes per task in
RoboHarn-Evo \[[291](#bib.bib232)\], and 20 tests per task in Robo-COP,
which doubles success on only one of three held-out
tasks \[[305](#bib.bib157)\]. Retention is measured only in the fixed
loops CRL-VLA and Simple Recipe \[[95](#bib.bib59), [161](#bib.bib60)\]
and approximated in self-evolving loops only by gates against
regression, the adoption test of Robo-COP and the risk gate of
Policy-Level RSI \[[305](#bib.bib157), [296](#bib.bib309)\]. As in
navigation, backbones confound cross-form comparison: training-free
loops mostly run frozen frontier models, weight-updating loops open
ones.

Tests outside the Writer.   Feedback acquisition sets the exposure of
consolidation, the two forms of writing differing in whether a test
outside the writer checks a write before it persists. Parametric writes
pass on the verifier’s score, inheriting the distribution shift of
frozen progress heads \[[19](#bib.bib149), [145](#bib.bib52),
[299](#bib.bib310)\] and the compounding hacking of co-trained
critics \[[298](#bib.bib158), [25](#bib.bib311)\], except where the
adoption test of Robo-COP or the risk gate of Policy-Level RSI adds a
test outside the update rule \[[305](#bib.bib157), [296](#bib.bib309)\].
Non-parametric writes pass tests at different distances from the writer,
from held-out seeds and fixed validation sets \[[289](#bib.bib202),
[190](#bib.bib151), [297](#bib.bib360)\] through execution
outcomes \[[290](#bib.bib203), [294](#bib.bib306), [293](#bib.bib305),
[292](#bib.bib304)\] to the writer’s own judgment \[[300](#bib.bib103),
[20](#bib.bib231), [301](#bib.bib303), [302](#bib.bib307)\]. A write
that only its writer checks persists with its errors, one SEAR run
saving a self-calibrated placement verifier and finishing at 4.6%
against 15.5% and 23.6% for two sibling runs without
it \[[20](#bib.bib231)\]. A test outside the writer matters even when it
checks only task success, the harness of Scale and Selection falling
from 40% to 0% over 20 rounds once every revision is accepted, whereas
champion-challenger selection raises held-out success from 51% to
67% \[[297](#bib.bib360)\]. The farther the test sits from the writer,
the more of the retained gain it protects.

### VII-D Limits and Preconditions

Bottleneck Attribution.   In embodied manipulation, both ceilings bind
fixed and self-evolving loops alike on hardware, self-reference changing
who supplies the goal, the score, or the write but not the cost or
attainable fidelity of a physical rollout. Fixed loops meet the same
ceilings, training against simulator success \[[62](#bib.bib161),
[287](#bib.bib162)\] or letting a separate model write memory or revise
a skill library \[[188](#bib.bib150), [309](#bib.bib308),
[310](#bib.bib401), [311](#bib.bib402)\]. The cost of self-reference
lies in what each entry point puts at risk: a success-conditioned choice
over a fixed library risks little, only the allocation following the
agent \[[21](#bib.bib155)\], whereas self-proposed practice moves
verification to checks the agent builds \[[20](#bib.bib231)\], a
co-trained critic lets its bias follow the policy \[[298](#bib.bib158),
[25](#bib.bib311)\], and a frozen model that judges and writes carries
one bias into both roles \[[300](#bib.bib103), [301](#bib.bib303)\].
Task choice and practice offset part of these costs, and only there are
controlled gains reported \[[21](#bib.bib155), [302](#bib.bib307)\].
Beyond these ablations, the costs rest on stage evidence and the
provenance in
[Table XII](#S7.T12 "In VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation").

Cross-Cycle Degradation.   Across cycles, self-reference opens paths
along which degradation follows the agent, and the environment path adds
the sim-to-real gap. On the goal side, success-conditioned task choice,
simplification, and failure-ranked collection open the goal
edge \[[21](#bib.bib155), [304](#bib.bib51), [296](#bib.bib309)\] and
self-proposed practice extends the agent edge into
$`\sigma_{\omega}`$ \[[302](#bib.bib307), [20](#bib.bib231),
[166](#bib.bib156), [298](#bib.bib158)\], both inviting curriculum
collapse. On the feedback side, co-trained critics extend the agent edge
into FA, inviting compounding reward hacking \[[298](#bib.bib158),
[25](#bib.bib311)\], and training a planner on videos of its co-trained
simulator invites model collapse \[[298](#bib.bib158)\], whereas frozen
progress heads stay off the agent edge yet admit distribution
shift \[[19](#bib.bib149)\]. The extension into UC carries erroneous
writes \[[20](#bib.bib231)\] and regression when every checkpoint is
deployed, below the frozen policy on three of the four tasks whose first
candidate its gate rejected \[[305](#bib.bib157)\], while the
environment path carries dynamics that loops closed in simulation never
score. Within reported budgets, regression and erroneous writes are
documented, whereas curriculum collapse, compounding reward hacking,
model collapse, and distribution shift remain inferred.

Presupposed Resources.   The mechanisms of embodied manipulation
presuppose resources that simulation supplies and hardware withholds.
Reinforcement learning against success presupposes simulator success
predicates \[[62](#bib.bib161)\], held-out gates simulated or deployment
trials \[[289](#bib.bib202), [305](#bib.bib157)\], learned hardware
feedback an audited judge \[[21](#bib.bib155), [173](#bib.bib160)\], and
written artifacts a test outside the writer \[[297](#bib.bib360),
[20](#bib.bib231)\].

## VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry

This section characterizes the cross-scenario asymmetry, in which the
two directions of a scenario pair receive different kinds of portability
verdict, a mechanism that applies in one scenario needing an adaptation,
being blocked, or becoming redundant in the other while the reverse
direction meets a different combination. We interpret the asymmetry
through two properties of each scenario, which factors are scarce there,
exogenously or through resources that self-reference gives up, and which
task-structural resources and conditions it holds, chiefly output
equivalence, checkable outcomes, and outcome observability. A mechanism
is portable on a target that holds the resource it presupposes,
conditional where that resource is held only on a sub-family or after an
adaptation, blocked where the outcome it judges or must check is
unobservable, and redundant where the factor it raises is not scarce.
The account concerns the kind of verdict each direction receives and
leaves aside cost differences across scenarios, which the
generation-verification gap would set. Quadrant placements and cost
comparisons are inferred from single-scenario evidence, and the verdicts
remain untested.

### VIII-A Exogenous and Endogenous Scarcity

A factor is scarce in a scenario where its value limits what a loop
gains, a condition that a binding ceiling implies but that a factor
without a ceiling can also meet. Scarcity is exogenous where it limits
fixed loops as well and endogenous where self-reference gives up a
resource that a fixed loop keeps, two reasons that comparing the
self-evolving and fixed loops of each scenario separates
([Secs. IV-D](#S4.SS4 "IV-D Limits and Preconditions ‣ IV Self-Evolution in Multimodal Reasoning"),
[V-D](#S5.SS4 "V-D Limits and Preconditions ‣ V Self-Evolution in Multimodal Generation"),
[VI-D](#S6.SS4 "VI-D Limits and Preconditions ‣ VI Self-Evolution in GUI and Web Navigation")
and [VII-D](#S7.SS4 "VII-D Limits and Preconditions ‣ VII Self-Evolution in Embodied Manipulation")).

Exogenous Scarcity.   Exogenous scarcity has two sources, the saturation
of $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ in every scenario and the low
ceilings of three. We infer the saturation from $`p_{g}(1-p_{g})`$
falling near zero where goals are mastered or out of reach. Generation
saturates from above, the fixed loop Flow-GRPO raising the GenEval score
of SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95 \[[195](#bib.bib173)\], and navigation and
manipulation from below, with initial navigation success below
20% \[[16](#bib.bib135), [135](#bib.bib139)\] and physical scenes that
afford only part of a task library \[[21](#bib.bib155)\]. Unbounded by
any ceiling, $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ counts as scarce in
every scenario. Fixed loops meet the low ceilings as well, scoring
open-ended images with learned preference models in
generation \[[195](#bib.bib173), [267](#bib.bib174), [312](#bib.bib403),
[313](#bib.bib404), [314](#bib.bib405), [315](#bib.bib406)\], paying
per-step environment latency in navigation \[[269](#bib.bib148)\], and
facing resets and success evaluation on hardware \[[21](#bib.bib155),
[188](#bib.bib150)\]. Self-reference leaves these ceilings in place,
changing who supplies the goal, the score, or the write and with it the
form of their cost.

Endogenous Scarcity.   Endogenous scarcity, the residual bottleneck we
place in multimodal reasoning, where neither ceiling is low, arises once
loops give up the answer keys that fixed loops keep. Fixed loops filter
rollouts by exact match against pre-collected keys, as in
M-STAR \[[152](#bib.bib49)\], whereas loops that pose or label their own
questions without a program to compute answers label by consensus or
self-judgment at a lower realized fidelity $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$. On 500
shared questions, VQS finds 24% of retained majority-vote labels and 18%
of retained model-judge labels wrong against 5.6% of retained
program-computed answers \[[64](#bib.bib176)\]. Self-posed goals also
give up scripts in SCALE \[[284](#bib.bib297)\] and
SEAR \[[20](#bib.bib231)\] without an endogenous scarcity of fidelity,
SCALE’s web end states remaining open to inspection and SEAR’s goals
staying in simulation, short of the hardware on which both ceilings
bind.
