### VIII-B Task-Structural Resources

Whether a meta-operator that the agent realizes can raise a scarce
factor varies across scenarios only with resources that the scenario
holds independently of the agent. We call *task structure* the part of a
scenario fixed before any choice of agent or meta-operator, namely the
environment family and evaluation distribution of the macro-environment
([Sec. II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"))
without its goal sampler, together with the interfaces through which a
loop resets, replicates, or inspects its environments, a property being
task-structural when replacing the agent and its three meta-operators
leaves it unchanged. *Task-structural resources* decide whether a
mechanism that presupposes them is defined or affordable, whereas
capabilities of the agent’s model and artifacts authored before the
loop, the two other kinds a mechanism can presuppose, hold on every
target.

Resources by Scenario.   Three task-structural resources recur across
the scenarios and are held unequally, output equivalence, checkable
outcomes, and resettable rollouts. Output equivalence, held by short
discrete answers but not by images or action trajectories, defines
majority voting without converting outputs into answers. Checkable
outcomes give each newly posed or reweighted goal its own reference
outside the agent, coming from keys, generation programs, state scripts,
or screen judges \[[152](#bib.bib49), [64](#bib.bib176),
[115](#bib.bib147), [14](#bib.bib42), [316](#bib.bib407),
[317](#bib.bib408), [318](#bib.bib409), [319](#bib.bib410)\].
Resettable, parallelizable rollouts let group sampling scale, at the
price of emulator and virtual-machine instances where episodes run in
software environments \[[14](#bib.bib42), [125](#bib.bib144)\].
Reasoning holds all three, navigation checkable outcomes and bought
rollouts, generation free rollouts with checks only on program-checkable
sub-families \[[195](#bib.bib173), [191](#bib.bib216)\], and
manipulation checks and bought rollouts only in
simulation \[[62](#bib.bib161)\], hardware episodes costing physical
time \[[19](#bib.bib149), [21](#bib.bib155)\]. The verdicts turn chiefly
on output equivalence and checkable outcomes, rollouts entering them
only through $`\bar{K}`$, which decides whether world models are
redundant. The ceilings of
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In III-D Stage 3: Update Consolidation (UC) ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")
reflect these resources only in part, navigation keeping a low
$`\bar{K}`$ under per-step latency despite resettable rollouts and
sharing a high $`\bar{F}`$ with reasoning, which alone holds output
equivalence. Portability is therefore derived from the resources of each
scenario, not read off its quadrant.

Observability and Online Checks.   Two further conditions decide whether
a held resource serves the loop, the observability of the outcome, which
task structure fixes, and an online check built on the resource, which
the loop’s design supplies or omits. The outcome is observable where it
appears in the agent’s observations or in a check available to the loop,
a condition that every mechanism judging or checking it presupposes. An
*online check*, a check built on a resource that runs inside the loop,
is the only route by which the resource lowers the realized cost of a
trade-off, and loops run one wherever answer keys, execution results, or
simulator outcomes are available, training-free methods checking their
writes against them \[[146](#bib.bib175), [201](#bib.bib298),
[290](#bib.bib203)\]. Holding a resource does not ensure such a check,
task streams, open prompts, and self-chosen practice tasks leaving none
even in navigation, as in WebCoach’s task stream \[[163](#bib.bib228)\].
The frozen acting model then judges its own episodes and writes the
update, as in ManimAgent \[[256](#bib.bib170)\],
Mobile-Agent-E \[[162](#bib.bib137)\], and SEAR \[[20](#bib.bib231)\],
and an error of judgment enters the update unchecked, one simulated SEAR
run saving a self-built verifier wrong on 91% of later rollouts. A loop
without an online check thus gives up a resource that its scenario
holds.

### VIII-C Trade-offs of Self-Evolving Mechanisms

[Table XIII](#S8.T13 "In VIII-A Exogenous and Endogenous Scarcity ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")
recasts the mechanisms of the scenario chapters as trade-offs, in which
an agent-realized meta-operator raises a factor by supplying what the
agent records, proposes, judges, or writes in place of a component fixed
before the loop. The goal sampler supplies the agent’s success record or
its own proposals in place of a fixed goal distribution, the feedback
function the agent’s judgment in place of an answer key or a checker,
and the evolution operator the agent’s authorship in place of an update
rule written in advance. Each trade-off pays what the supplied output
lacks relative to the replaced component and presupposes a resource that
is task-structural, a capability of the agent’s model, or an artifact
authored before the loop. Of its three elements, the factor raised, the
resource presupposed, and the price paid, only the first two enter the
portability verdicts.

Experience Generation.   The mechanisms of experience generation raise
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$, scarce in every scenario, and
differ in what they give up to raise it, with a learned world model as
the one exception. Success-conditioned allocation reweights a fixed task
set, giving up coverage of the tasks it down-weights and presupposing
checkable outcomes on that set. Created goals, posed by the agent or
generated from its record, extend the factor beyond a fixed pool but
give up the answer key or checking script of each pooled goal,
presupposing in its place an outcome that something other than their
generator can check or answers that a vote can compare.
Program-checkable goal families keep the check by creating goals only
where a program answers or renders them, as in VQS \[[64](#bib.bib176)\]
and RSI in UMMs \[[191](#bib.bib216)\], giving up coverage of
$`\mathcal{G}`$ outside the family. A learned world model, the one
mechanism that replaces a component of the environment and not a fixed
component of a meta-operator, instead raises $`K_{k}`$, replacing the
environment dynamics $`P`$ with imagined rollouts that $`\bar{K}`$ does
not bound and presupposing dynamics learnable over short horizons, the
trade-off that model-based reinforcement learning has analyzed from
Dyna \[[320](#bib.bib315)\] to MBPO \[[321](#bib.bib314)\]. It enters
the loop through $`V_{\nu}`$, its imagined outcomes scored by a reward
or value head \[[25](#bib.bib311), [299](#bib.bib310)\] or by the
agent’s own judge \[[298](#bib.bib158)\], and model error thus reaches
$`F_{\nu}`$.

Feedback Acquisition.   Each feedback mechanism pays for the substituted
judgment in fidelity, its gain depending on the evaluator it replaces,
and the mechanisms fall into three groups by the kind of resource they
presuppose, the distinction on which their verdicts turn. The
self-consistency vote raises $`F_{\nu}`$ without keys at a price of
several rollouts per goal and presupposes output equivalence together
with a prior concentrated on the true answer. Self-judgment and
generator-confidence rewards raise $`F_{\nu}`$ without checkers and
presuppose only capabilities of the agent’s model, a
generation-verification gap or the generator’s confidence, which hold on
every target, the gap pricing these rewards without deciding where they
port. Verifiers refit on the agent’s trajectories and frozen
self-derived estimators raise $`L_{\nu}`$ besides $`F_{\nu}`$ and
presuppose an artifact authored before the loop, a labeled seed, a
reference set, or demonstrations.

Update Consolidation.   Update consolidation contributes one trade-off,
episode reuse through memory, skills, or harnesses, which raises
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ on goals initially out of reach and,
where a written library carries beyond $`\mathcal{G}_{k}`$, also
$`G_{\zeta}`$, paying in exposure to the writer’s errors. It presupposes
either the writer’s generation-verification gap, a capability held on
every target, or an online check that gates the writes, as keys and
validation sets do in training-free reasoning
loops \[[146](#bib.bib175), [225](#bib.bib286), [222](#bib.bib285)\].
Weight updates under a rule fixed before the loop supply no agent
authorship and enter the trade-offs only through the feedback they
consume.

### VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources

The evidence on the price paid, the trade-off element the verdicts leave
out, serves the account in two ways, setting the cost of the conditional
routes the verdicts open and bearing on whether a factor other than
scarcity and resources could produce the asymmetry. The comparisons
below each stay inside one paper, bearing on a mechanism’s gain and,
where measured, its cost. Degradation, the rest of the cost, is left
aside, its evidence too uneven for cross-scenario comparison.

Generation-Verification Gap.   The generation-verification gap prices a
trade-off wherever the agent’s own judgment serves as the reference, as
a capability that holds on every target
([Sec. VIII-C](#S8.SS3 "VIII-C Trade-offs of Self-Evolving Mechanisms ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")),
and remains inferred in multimodal loops. Introduced for language
models, the gap is the improvement a model obtains by filtering or
reweighting its own generations with its own
verification \[[322](#bib.bib312)\]. We extend the term by separating a
task-level component, the difference in difficulty between verifying and
generating on a task family, from a model-level component, the
difference between the verification and generation accuracy of the
agent’s own model on the same goals. The model-level component remains
unestimated, multimodal audits reporting only the verification
side \[[64](#bib.bib176), [256](#bib.bib170), [281](#bib.bib145)\], and
backbone priors would confound it even once measured
([Sec. III-E](#S3.SS5 "III-E Cross-Scenario Positioning ‣ III The Three-Stage Self-Evolving Loop")).
We infer the task-level component to be large in GUI and Web navigation,
where a final screen can be inspected without replaying the steps that
reach it, and small in open-prompt generation, where judging whether an
image satisfies a prompt calls on the compositional understanding that
producing it requires, a difference that makes the cost of self-judgment
vary across scenarios even where its verdict does not.

Evaluator Fidelity.   The feedback ablations order evaluators by
fidelity and thereby price the conditional routes that substitute a
judge for a missing check. Two ablations, both in generation, compare a
verifier built on the agent’s own judgment with the evaluator it
replaces, a frozen self-rater against a program check in one and a
co-trained reward model against a learned preference scorer in the
other. In RSI in UMMs, training on the better of two images as rated by
the frozen starting model gains 0.5 points, against 8.6 points with
execution-verified charts for the same requests and
steps \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. The reward model that The Image as Its Own
Reward \[[245](#bib.bib172)\] co-trains against reference images matches
the PickScore of Flow-GRPO \[[195](#bib.bib173)\] trained on PickScore
and wins 70.0% of the authors’ human image-quality comparisons against
it, a model that the same raters place below its base. A verifier built
on the agent’s own judgment thus falls below a program check and can
exceed a learned preference scorer, an ordering whose two ends come from
different verifiers, one frozen and one co-trained, and which the other
scenarios leave untested. The ordering would be contradicted if such a
verifier outperformed a keyed or programmatic check at a matched budget
on fixed goals.

Goal-Mechanism Gains.   Goal mechanisms gain in all four scenarios with
one reported exception, consistent with a scarcity of
$`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ that gives this factor no part in
the asymmetry. Removing allocation hurts both scenarios that ablate it,
MobileRL \[[17](#bib.bib293)\] losing 6.3 points of AndroidWorld success
without its failure curriculum filter and Policy-Level
RSI \[[296](#bib.bib309)\] raising its ManiSkill failure rate from 2.34%
to 3.36% under random scene selection. Created goals lead untrained,
random, or frozen-source generators in VisPlay \[[5](#bib.bib45)\],
RATs \[[302](#bib.bib307)\], ACuRL \[[15](#bib.bib299)\], and
RSIgen \[[260](#bib.bib218)\], and trail the NNetNav curriculum by 1.3
points in one SEAgent setting \[[16](#bib.bib135)\]. Within a
program-checkable family the error-driven chart distribution of RSI in
UMMs leads a fixed distribution with the same number of verified charts
by 2.8 to 4.1 points in every round \[[191](#bib.bib216)\]. These
comparisons come from the authors of each method and may overstate the
gain, yet their agreement across the four scenarios leaves the verdicts
on goal mechanisms to turn on the resources they presuppose.

Writer Dependence.   The gain of reuse depends on the writer, a
model-level dependence that travels with the agent to every target and
adds no asymmetry of its own. Authored writes outperform skill-free or
raw alternatives in two navigation ablations,
EvoSkill-GUI \[[281](#bib.bib145)\] gaining 6.7 points on MobileWorld
over pass@3 without skills and Agent S \[[278](#bib.bib294)\] 7.7 points
on an OSWorld subset over full trajectories in place of its
self-evaluator’s summaries. SEAR \[[20](#bib.bib231)\], holding the
scenario fixed and varying only the writer, finds the sign of this gain
reversed, GPT-5.6-sol on RoboLab dropping from 46.9% without a library
to 42.4% with its own, beyond the spread of three runs, and rising to
60.6% with one that Claude Opus 5 wrote, a loss the authors trace to
object-location recipes with few grasp checks. Whether such content
tracks the generation-verification gap of the writer’s model is
untested, and a library that gained the same whoever wrote it would
contradict the dependence on the writer.

### VIII-E Directed Portability across Scenario Pairs

The two directions of each scenario pair receive verdicts of different
kinds, a difference traced to which factors are scarce and which
task-structural resources and conditions hold. The direction from $`X`$
to $`Y`$ collects the mechanisms portable or conditional in $`X`$ that
on $`Y`$ are redundant or rank lower in the order portable, conditional,
blocked, and reversing the pair exchanges both the mechanisms carried
and the conditions they meet. A mechanism whose verdict does not fall
belongs to neither direction by construction, and the asymmetry
accordingly concerns the kind of obstacle a direction meets, not how
many mechanisms transfer.
[Table XIV](#S8.T14 "In VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")
assigns per-target verdicts by the rules below.

Verdict Rules.   The rules apply in a fixed order, observability first,
a mechanism that judges or checks an unobservable outcome being blocked
whatever its other conditions, then scarcity, which decides redundancy,
and resources last, which decide between portable and conditional. A
mechanism is *redundant* where the factor it raises is not scarce,
judged at the ceiling or, where the loop gives up a resource, at the
realized value, as for self-labeled questions without keys and task
streams without online checks. $`\mathbb{E}[I_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}]`$ and
$`G_{\zeta}`$, neither bounded by a ceiling, count as scarce everywhere
([Sec. VIII-A](#S8.SS1 "VIII-A Exogenous and Endogenous Scarcity ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")),
and $`L_{\nu}`$ as not scarce where a single action fixes
$`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$. Otherwise a mechanism is *portable* where the target
holds the resource it presupposes and *conditional* where an adaptation,
such as converting outputs into answers or adding an external judge, or
a sub-family supplies it, a missing resource admitting such a route in
the surveyed targets wherever the outcome is observable. Capabilities of
the agent’s model and artifacts authored before the loop count as held
everywhere
([Sec. VIII-B](#S8.SS2 "VIII-B Task-Structural Resources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")).
Where the outcome is unobservable, observability caps the verdict and
every mechanism that judges or checks it is *blocked*, even those
presupposing only the agent’s model, whereas low evaluator accuracy only
raises the cost of a conditional route. A portable verdict states that a
precondition holds, not that a transfer improves the target loop.

Redundant Verdicts.   Redundant verdicts fall on world models where
rollouts are cheap and on feedback mechanisms where an external
reference already supplies every factor they raise. Reasoning and
generation keep $`\bar{K}`$ high through a single decoding or sampling
pass, leaving world models redundant there. The vote, self-judgment, and
generator-confidence rewards are redundant on reasoning questions with
keys or program-computed answers and on navigation goals whose outcome a
check inspects online. Self-judging navigation loops such as Agent
S \[[278](#bib.bib294)\] and Mobile-Agent-E \[[162](#bib.bib137)\], by
contrast, run on task streams or practice goals whose screen-visible
outcomes no check inspects, leaving $`F_{\nu}`$ scarce at the realized
value and self-judgment portable. Refit verifiers and frozen estimators
are redundant only on these reasoning questions, where one action fixes
$`L_{\nu}\!=\!1`$, multi-step navigation and manipulation keeping
$`L_{\nu}`$ scarce.

Conditional Verdicts.   Conditional verdicts arise where the target
holds a presupposed task-structural resource only on a sub-family or
through an adaptation. Allocation and program-checkable families are
conditional where checks cover only a sub-family, as in
generation \[[11](#bib.bib163), [191](#bib.bib216)\] and on hardware,
where an external judge grades a task library \[[21](#bib.bib155)\] or a
scripted scene check covers a fixed family \[[323](#bib.bib313)\].
Created goals, checkable in reasoning and navigation, find a check in
generation only through image questions, rendered charts, or external
judges \[[40](#bib.bib166), [191](#bib.bib216), [260](#bib.bib218)\]. On
hardware, agent-posed goals stay in simulation \[[302](#bib.bib307),
[20](#bib.bib231)\], and the external judge of before-and-after images
under which SEAR practices given tasks offers a route where success
shows as object motion, a case FailBench finds nearly
solved \[[324](#bib.bib194)\]. World models find learnable dynamics on
hardware only over short horizons \[[24](#bib.bib154)\] and in
navigation only over text-rendered web states, as in
DynaWeb \[[325](#bib.bib100)\]. Outside the discrete answers of
reasoning, the vote finds output equivalence only through questions that
turn outputs into comparable answers, as ASG poses about generated
images \[[40](#bib.bib166)\], a conversion untested on final screens and
camera frames.

Blocked Verdicts.   Blocked verdicts arise where the outcome of a goal
appears neither in the agent’s observations nor in any check available
to the loop, as for background-state goals in navigation that no
reachable screen shows and no script inspects. Contact-rich assembly is
the candidate sub-family on hardware, where no judge in FailBench
exceeds 0.60 balanced accuracy against 0.77 for the best judge overall,
a result consistent with frames that omit the contact on which success
depends, although the authors also name task-specific knowledge and
precision \[[324](#bib.bib194)\]. On such goals the vote and
self-judgment have nothing to judge, recorded actions showing what the
agent did and not whether the state changed, created goals have nothing
to check them, and success-conditioned allocation has no success record
to read, a block reaching model-only mechanisms as well as
resource-dependent ones. Refit verifiers and frozen estimators keep the
progress that visible steps show, and episode reuse the writes that need
no judgment of success, both becoming conditional there, whereas
generator-confidence rewards, which never judge the outcome, stay
portable at their cost in fidelity, a verdict certifying only that their
precondition holds while their fidelity on outcomes that nothing
observes stays unknown. No reported instance falls in a blocked cell,
leaving the rules consistent yet unsupported.

Asymmetry by Target.   The kind of verdict that a direction meets is
fixed chiefly by its target, and the two directions of a pair differ
wherever their targets differ in scarcity, resources, or observability.
Checkable outcomes act on both sides of the pair of navigation and
generation, the judges of generation becoming redundant on navigation
goals that a check inspects online and the created goals of navigation
becoming conditional on the open prompts of generation. Reasoning and
manipulation show the pattern most sharply, the vote and the goal
mechanisms carried from reasoning becoming conditional on hardware and,
program-checkable families aside, blocked where contact decides success,
while the world models and estimators of manipulation become redundant
on reasoning questions with keys or program-computed answers
([Table XIV](#S8.T14 "In VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")).
More broadly, directions into reasoning meet only redundancy, directions
into generation and hardware chiefly conditional goal mechanisms and
votes, and where the outcome is unobservable, navigation and hardware
block goal mechanisms and judges from every source, a verdict that
depends on the target alone
([Figure 4](#S8.F4 "In VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")).

Structural Source.   Taken together, we interpret the structural source
of the asymmetry as two scenario properties that the directions of a
pair meet in different combinations, the scarcity that $`\bar{K}`$ and
$`\bar{F}`$ fix, read at the realized value where a loop gives up a
resource, and the unequal task structure, comprising its resources and
the observability of its outcomes. Scarcity decides redundancy,
task-structural resources decide between portable and conditional
verdicts, and observability alone decides blocking. Observability is
also the one task-structural condition that bounds mechanisms
presupposing only the agent’s model. Matrix positions anticipate most
verdicts, failing where output equivalence or observability decides
them, as for the vote and background-state goals in navigation. Still
untested, the verdicts would fall to a gain over an equal-budget control
for an unadapted mechanism lacking its resource, one raising a
non-scarce factor, or one judging unobservable outcomes.

This section reviews how self-evolving multimodal agents are evaluated
on task-solving capability, on self-evolving capability, and through the
judges and reward models that supply their feedback, and identifies the
measurements whose absence leaves our account untestable.

### IX-A Task-Solving Capability

Task-solving capability, the expected return $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$
([Eq. 6](#S2.E6 "In II-B Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent ‣ II Preliminaries"))
that an agent attains on the goals of a scenario with its components
fixed, is measured on task-specific benchmarks that fix a goal set, any
environment that rollouts need, and usually a scorer
([Table XV](#S9.T15 "In IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")).
A reported score estimates $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ only insofar as the goal
set represents $`\mu_{\mathcal{G}}`$ and the scorer agrees with $`R`$,
and audits find both conditions broken. The goal set fails through
memorization, Sphinx-X-MoE reaching 43.6% on MMMU \[[327](#bib.bib337)\]
without images, 17.9 points above its language-model
backbone \[[359](#bib.bib372)\] and vision-language-action models above
90% on LIBERO \[[348](#bib.bib196)\] falling to 0.0% under the
perturbations of LIBERO-PRO \[[349](#bib.bib343)\]. The scorer fails
through divergence and exploits, GenEval \[[334](#bib.bib333)\]
deviating from human judgment by up to 17.7
points \[[360](#bib.bib373)\] and BenchJack \[[361](#bib.bib374)\]
reaching near-perfect scores on most of ten agent benchmarks without
solving a task. A loop that trains with the scorer it is evaluated by,
as Reflection-VLA \[[304](#bib.bib51)\] does on LIBERO, can write
memorized goals and scorer errors into the agent, a self-evolving agent
thus being more exposed to these failures than the static models and
agents that the audits examine.

### IX-B Self-Evolving Capability

Self-evolving capability, the ability to raise $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ over
the cycles of a loop, is measured by self-evolution benchmarks that fix
the goals, the environment, any feedback, and the schedule in which the
agent attempts and is tested on goals
([Table XVI](#S9.T16 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")),
whereas loops on task-specific benchmarks report $`\mathcal{J}_{k}`$ by
round or only at the endpoints. Text-only benchmarks apply the same
protocol to memory, lifelong-learning, and harness-evolution streams and
to professional workflows \[[362](#bib.bib104), [363](#bib.bib182),
[364](#bib.bib412), [365](#bib.bib183), [366](#bib.bib105),
[367](#bib.bib243), [368](#bib.bib244), [369](#bib.bib332),
[370](#bib.bib241), [371](#bib.bib242), [372](#bib.bib184),
[373](#bib.bib181), [374](#bib.bib179), [375](#bib.bib239),
[376](#bib.bib411), [377](#bib.bib240), [378](#bib.bib180)\], whereas
benchmarks in which the agent remembers supplied
histories \[[379](#bib.bib413), [380](#bib.bib195),
[381](#bib.bib414)\], learns from supplied demonstrations or labeled
streams \[[382](#bib.bib319), [383](#bib.bib415)\], or is scored without
updating itself \[[384](#bib.bib106)\] fall outside this measurement,
leaving no update that follows from the agent’s own outcomes.
Independent scores across rounds trace the increment
$`\Delta\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{J}_{k+1}-\mathcal{J}_{k}`$, cumulative
scores mix it with resampling, endpoint comparisons give only the total
gain, and re-tests of earlier goals and held-out goals bear on retention
$`S_{\zeta}`$ and generalization $`G_{\zeta}`$. A gain counts as
evidence of the capability only to the extent that controls separate the
agent’s experience from added computation, repeated attempts, writing
itself, and run variance, as in MemGUI-Bench \[[385](#bib.bib316)\],
where retries alone raise M3A by 14.9 points while removing the
long-term memory of Agent-S2 at the same three attempts costs it 20.0
points. Whether the check reaches the agent also shapes the gain,
conditions that withhold it lowering gains or leaving them
mixed \[[386](#bib.bib331), [387](#bib.bib329)\], with late-round
successes in PhysRSI-eval falling from 15 to 5 of 36 without the
grader \[[388](#bib.bib323)\], whereas the protocols marked ^(†) return
the check, a gain under them possibly including its exploitation, as
exposing a simulator’s success criteria to embodied agents yields gains
that vanish once the criteria change slightly \[[389](#bib.bib419)\].
These benchmarks measure mechanisms only on goals whose outcomes are
checked, away from the goals where
[Table XIV](#S8.T14 "In VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")
sets verdicts by missing checks or unobservable outcomes, and cover
navigation and manipulation, on hardware only in SEAR’s five
tasks \[[20](#bib.bib231)\], with reasoning and generation covered only
by Flex-RSI \[[390](#bib.bib418)\], which omits navigation.

### IX-C Judges and Reward Models

Where no answer key or program checks an output, a self-evolving agent
realizes $`V_{\nu}`$ through a judge or a reward model, whose
preferences $`f_{\zeta}`$ writes into $`\mathcal{A}_{k+1}`$ while the
loop observes no $`R`$, moving the policy toward outputs that the scorer
overrates. A scorer that shares the updated parameters or is refit moves
with the policy as well. Evaluations compare these scorers with a
reference outside the loop
([Table XVII](#S9.T17 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation"))
and bear on the realized fidelity $`F_{\nu}^{(k)}`$ only insofar as
their outputs and scorer resemble those in the loop. On fixed outputs,
agreement stays moderate and falls off the training distribution, the
strongest judges reaching 62.9%–72% accuracy \[[391](#bib.bib188),
[392](#bib.bib189), [393](#bib.bib354), [285](#bib.bib192)\], reward
models dropping to near chance on pairs outside their training
data \[[135](#bib.bib139), [394](#bib.bib350)\], and a log that reports
success misleading judges on failed clips \[[395](#bib.bib363)\].
Optimization exposes further errors, reward hacking reaching 48.1% for
VQA policies \[[396](#bib.bib205)\] and a judge passing repairs that
humans mostly reject \[[395](#bib.bib363)\], although a fixed screen
judge stays accurate on the policy trained against
it \[[15](#bib.bib299)\] and fixed-output accuracy largely orders
scorers by the downstream results of policies optimized against
them \[[142](#bib.bib193), [397](#bib.bib191)\]. References that check
outcomes reach open-ended outputs only through single-property
interventions \[[398](#bib.bib348)\], leaving such outputs scored
against human labels, larger models, or other reward
models \[[396](#bib.bib205), [399](#bib.bib197), [400](#bib.bib318)\].

### IX-D Measurement Gaps

We list a measurement as missing only where its absence leaves one of
three claims untestable, that a method’s gain comes from self-evolution,
that a scenario sits where we place it on the positioning matrix, and
that the portability verdicts hold, the last two specific to our
account. These measurements share the need for a reference the loop
never receives, a reference returned to the agent entering its feedback
$`V_{\nu}`$ and becoming exploitable by its updates.

Attribution of Gains.   Attributing a gain to self-evolution requires,
in every scenario, the increment across rounds against a non-evolving
baseline at a matched budget and, where the scorer that checks updates
also produces the reported score, a reference withheld from the loop.
Four self-evolution benchmarks run this baseline
([Table XVI](#S9.T16 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")),
Flex-RSI among them with harness edits raising the test score in six of
seven paired runs \[[390](#bib.bib418)\], as does
RATs \[[302](#bib.bib307)\], whereas the other comparisons reported in
reasoning and generation, such as V-Zero against supervised
GRPO \[[7](#bib.bib46)\], state no matched budget. On hardware the
budget also counts the human resets that $`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$ admits,
which Find Something You Can’t Do records as scene
recoveries \[[21](#bib.bib155)\], lest an evolving arm draw on more of
them than its baseline. The withheld reference, such as the test split
that Flex-RSI scores once after each run \[[390](#bib.bib418)\],
separates the gain from exploitation of the scorer, as for the protocols
marked ^(†), and, where training and reported goals coincide, from
memorization. Agreement on fixed outputs ranks scorers without bounding
that exploitation, and the audits in
[Table XVII](#S9.T17 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")
cover parameter updates and single-output repair, leaving exploitation
through memory and tool writes untested.

Scenario Placement.   Placing a scenario depends only on whether each
ceiling is low or high, and a misplacement would merely move verdicts
into or out of the redundant class. Rollout cost in a common unit would
test the split on $`\bar{K}`$, yet the reported units do not convert,
ranging from tokens in MemGUI-Bench to hours of robot time in
Self-Improving EFMs \[[19](#bib.bib149)\]. The split on $`\bar{F}`$
remains inferred, the evaluations of
[Table XVII](#S9.T17 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")
defining each reference within one scenario and values taken from fixed
outputs erring in either direction. A higher $`\bar{F}`$ than we place
in generation or on hardware would make the feedback mechanisms there
redundant, and for generation the references on optimized outputs reduce
to human labels in a simulated repair loop \[[395](#bib.bib363)\] and,
under retraining, other reward models \[[408](#bib.bib375)\].

Verdict Testing.   Testing a verdict of
[Table XIV](#S8.T14 "In VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")
means running the matched-budget comparison in the target scenario with
the mechanism moved unadapted, on goals outside the self-evolution
benchmarks wherever the verdict turns on missing checks or unobservable
outcomes. A conditional verdict also needs the adapted arm, and a
blocked verdict an outcome check held outside the loop, one available to
the loop making the outcome observable. Where a loop gives up a
resource, the verdict rests on realized $`F_{\nu}`$, whose test needs
the policy optimized against a scorer that changes with it, a joint
condition that
[Table XVII](#S9.T17 "In IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")
checks against a hidden key only in text \[[409](#bib.bib185)\]. The
reported transfers fall short of such a test, ASG \[[40](#bib.bib166)\]
bringing voting to generation without an unadapted arm,
failure-conditioned curricula moving from the text-only
WebRL \[[410](#bib.bib41)\] to screen-based loops \[[16](#bib.bib135),
[15](#bib.bib299)\] only within navigation, and SEAR starting its
hardware tasks from an empty library instead of the one written in
simulation. The verdicts thus remain untested under a shared protocol.

## X Open Challenges

This section discusses four open problems: reference construction,
self-derived verification, and cross-substrate transfer, which inform
our account of the cross-scenario asymmetry, along with safety under
autonomy, which bears on the operational definition of self-evolution.

### X-A Reference Construction

Reference construction, the building of a substitute reference for an
outcome absent from both the agent’s observations and every check
available to the loop, decides whether the blocked verdicts can be
lifted, as for background-state goals in navigation and possibly
contact-rich assembly on hardware
([Sec. VIII-E](#S8.SS5 "VIII-E Directed Portability across Scenario Pairs ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry")),
and the four reported routes each succeed only in part. Converting
outputs into answers \[[40](#bib.bib166)\] needs an equivalence relation
that screens and action trajectories lack, and a program written
together with the goal covers only goal families with a closed-form
success condition, EvoCUA resolving by hand the synthesized tasks on
which its two checks disagree \[[416](#bib.bib141)\]. A learned world
model adds its own prediction error, its dynamics learned on hardware
only over short horizons \[[24](#bib.bib154)\] and in navigation only
over text-rendered states \[[325](#bib.bib100)\], while a
vision-language judge reads camera frames that do not record contact
forces \[[324](#bib.bib194)\]. Whether a loop can construct such a
reference without a human inside the loop thus remains open, an
affirmative answer turning the blocked verdicts into conditional ones
that depend on how the reference is built and a negative one making the
block a property of the outcome itself.

### X-B Self-Derived Verification

Self-derived verification, the scoring of outcomes or steps by a
verifier derived from the agent’s own model or trajectories, is adopted
wherever no check scores an outcome or a check returns one verdict per
long episode, and its reliability turns on how far the verifier depends
on the policy. Verifiers that change with the policy drift or inherit
its errors, confidence rewards collapsing in ablated configurations of
SOLACE \[[9](#bib.bib63)\] and IRIS \[[129](#bib.bib165)\] and step
reward models trained on the agent’s trajectories inheriting its
mistakes \[[135](#bib.bib139), [144](#bib.bib143)\]. Lagged, co-trained,
and frozen verifiers, such as the moving-average teacher of
UniEvo-VL \[[263](#bib.bib291)\], the initial model in
PRISM \[[247](#bib.bib168)\], and progress heads frozen before
reinforcement learning \[[19](#bib.bib149), [145](#bib.bib52)\], depend
on the policy less or not at all, trading a moving bias for one fixed by
their source, a trade that no report compares across degrees of
dependence. Whether any degree of dependence keeps a verifier consistent
with $`R`$ once the policy leaves the support on which the verifier was
formed remains open, an affirmative answer making reliability a choice
of dependence and supplying step-level credit to long episodes, and a
negative one turning the low $`\bar{F}`$ of generation and hardware and
the scarcity of $`L_{\nu}`$ in navigation and manipulation into
structural limits.

### X-C Cross-Substrate Transfer

Cross-substrate transfer, the carrying of what a loop writes, whether a
skill library, a harness, or a policy, to another reader, platform, or
embodiment once the missing resources are supplied, underlies the
conditional verdicts for hardware targets, and the reported evidence
leaves it unsettled. Across platforms, zero-shot transfer is reported
only for the fixed loop GUI-HARVEST, whose harness evolved on OSWorld
raises GPT-5 by 13.87 points on
WindowsAgentArena \[[286](#bib.bib301)\]. Across simulators and action
interfaces, the code policies of SEAR lose little while its VLA policies
lose most of their success, the former falling from 33.3% to 28.7% and
the latter from 43.1% to 10.2% \[[20](#bib.bib231)\]. Across readers,
the same WebCoach memory lowers a 7B agent and raises larger
ones \[[163](#bib.bib228)\], in line with the writer dependence of
[Sec. VIII-D](#S8.SS4 "VIII-D Costs and Alternative Sources ‣ VIII Cross-Scenario Asymmetry").
No report carries a write across the simulation-to-hardware boundary,
SEAR starting its hardware tasks from an empty library
([Sec. IX-D](#S9.SS4 "IX-D Measurement Gaps ‣ IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation")).
Whether a write takes effect across readers, platforms, and embodiments,
the simulation-to-hardware boundary included, without new experience
accordingly remains open, an affirmative answer loosening the
conditional verdicts for hardware targets and a negative one making the
substrate itself a missing resource there.

### X-D Safety under Autonomy

Autonomy ($`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$) excludes human veto from the loop,
leaving the loop itself to preserve safety across modifications, as the
first of the three laws proposed for self-evolving agents
requires \[[28](#bib.bib4)\], and the reported evidence shows safety
eroding along each path of self-modification examined. Degradation is
reported along the model, memory, tool, and workflow paths, on text and
code except for one screen-based case, SEAgent, whose unsafe completion
rate on RiOSWorld rises from 39.5% to 55.3% \[[417](#bib.bib320)\].
Experience accumulated only on benign tasks in text-rendered web and
embodied environments raises attack success on later high-risk
tasks \[[418](#bib.bib321)\], and safety-oriented loops such as
FailBank \[[419](#bib.bib322)\] draw their proposals from a teacher
fixed before the loop, leaving untouched the loops in which the agent
supplies its own feedback. Whether a loop can preserve a safety property
across cycles while no human input reaches its goals, feedback, updates,
or actions remains open, an affirmative answer showing autonomy and
safety need not trade off under $`\mathcal{C}_{1}`$ and a negative one
making the trade-off a consequence of the definition, common to all
scenarios.

## XI Conclusion

Summary.  This survey investigates the structural source of
cross-scenario asymmetry in mechanism portability across four scenarios.
Through the three-stage self-evolving loop, we place the four scenarios
in a positioning matrix spanned by ceilings on rollout count and
feedback fidelity, and use fixed loops to separate scenario-imposed
limits from those incurred by self-evolving design. We then recast each
mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a
task-structural resource, and attribute the asymmetry to the different
combinations of scarce factors and resources that the two directions of
a scenario pair encounter. Inferred from single-scenario evidence, the
resulting portability verdicts are testable preconditions, not empirical
guarantees.
[Sec. IX](#S9 "IX Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent Evaluation") identifies
the measurements that would test them, and
[Sec. X](#S10 "X Open Challenges") discusses the problems that existing
mechanisms leave open.

Limitations.  Although this survey characterizes the cross-scenario
asymmetry through an explicit definition, framework, and set of verdict
rules, it has the following limitations. First, inclusion requires the
agent to realize at least one of the goal sampler, the feedback
function, or the evolution operator, a criterion that confines the
scenario patterns to the self-evolving subset and admits fixed loops
only as controls. The provenance assignments and the grouping axes of
the scenario taxonomies were made by a single coder, the axes after the
binding constraints had been identified, and the consolidation profiles
partly reflect which scenarios report retention and generalization at
all. Second, the quadrant placement rests on single-scenario estimates
of rollout cost and feedback fidelity that do not separate the
pretraining coverage of the backbone from the task structure, and the
verdicts are derived from rules, not observed in transfer experiments.
Third, the three-stage decomposition is one of several possible stage
boundaries, and credit assignment, treated here as a refinement of
feedback acquisition, could instead form a separate stage. Finally, the
surveyed methods center on image, video, screen, and robot-camera
inputs, leaving loops with audio, tactile, or force feedback unexamined,
and later work, particularly in embodied manipulation, may revise the
placements and verdicts.
